acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
A hydrogen nucleus (a single proton) has a diameter of about $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$.

$t = \dfrac{d}{c} \approx \dfrac{10^{-15}}{3\times10^{8}} \approx 3\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s}$, so the best estimate is $10^{-23}\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Far too long: light travels about 30 m in $10^{-7}\ \mathrm{s}$.
perOption.B: Light travels about $3\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ in this time, far larger than a nucleus.
perOption.C: Corresponds to about $3\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, roughly the size of an atom, not its nucleus.
perOption.D: Correct. $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m} \div 3\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \sim 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{s}$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
The weight of the whole body acts at its centre of gravity. The body balances only if the line of action of the weight passes through the support, so the weight has zero moment about the support.

The support's normal force also acts through the support, so the resultant torque is zero and the resultant force (weight minus normal force) is zero.

perOption.A: For a non-uniform body, equal masses on each side do not give equal moments; it is moments, not masses, that must balance.
perOption.B: A non-uniform body's centre of gravity is generally not at its geometric centre, so balancing there would leave a resultant torque.
perOption.C: Correct. Weight acts through the pivot, so it has no moment about it.
perOption.D: The force by the body on the support acts on the support, not on the body; equilibrium needs the support's force on the body to balance the weight (and zero torque).

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
Let each string make a small angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. Resolving vertically at the junction: $2T\sin\theta = W$, so $T = \dfrac{W}{2\sin\theta}$.

Since the strings are almost horizontal, $\sin\theta$ is very small (less than $\tfrac12$ once $\theta < 30^\circ$), so $T > W$.

perOption.A: $T$ can never be less than $W/2$; that would need $\sin\theta > 1$.
perOption.B: $T = W/2$ only if the strings are vertical ($\theta = 90^\circ$), not almost horizontal.
perOption.C: This range applies for $30^\circ \le \theta < 90^\circ$, not for nearly horizontal strings.
perOption.D: Correct. $T = W/(2\sin\theta)$ and small $\theta$ makes $T$ much larger than $W$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
All the gravitational PE lost becomes elastic PE in the spring (smooth surface, no losses):

$mgh = \tfrac12 kx^2 \Rightarrow x = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mgh}{k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.22)(9.81)(0.40)}{350}} = 7.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: This is $x^2 = 4.9\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}$; the square root was not taken.
perOption.B: Too small; comes from mishandling the units or the energy equation (e.g. using $h$ in cm wrongly or dropping a factor).
perOption.C: Too small; results from an algebra slip in rearranging $\tfrac12 kx^2 = mgh$.
perOption.D: Correct. $x = \sqrt{2mgh/k} = 0.070\ \mathrm{m}$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Without air resistance, the only force is weight, so the acceleration is $g$ for any mass.

Vertical motion from the same height with zero initial vertical velocity gives the same time $t$; horizontal velocity $v$ is unchanged, so the range $d = vt$ is the same.

perOption.A: Correct. Mass does not affect the motion when air resistance is negligible.
perOption.B: The horizontal velocity is the same and there is no horizontal force, so the range does not decrease.
perOption.C: Acceleration is $g$ regardless of mass, so the heavier ball does not fall faster.
perOption.D: Both time and distance are independent of mass; this assumes heavier objects fall faster.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
The seat must provide a vertical component $mg$ (to balance weight) and a horizontal component $ma = 0.50\,mg$ (to accelerate the child).

$F = \sqrt{(mg)^2 + (0.50\,mg)^2} = \sqrt{1.25}\,mg \approx 1.1\,mg$.

perOption.A: This is only the horizontal component that accelerates the child.
perOption.B: This is only the vertical component that balances the weight.
perOption.C: Correct. Vector sum of $mg$ and $0.50\,mg$ is $1.1\,mg$.
perOption.D: Adds the two perpendicular components as scalars instead of as vectors.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
With the period fixed, $\omega = 2\pi/T$ is unchanged.

$a = r\omega^2$, so doubling $r$ doubles $a$.

perOption.A: Results from thinking $a \propto r^2$, e.g. using $v^2$ with $v \propto r$ but forgetting to divide by $r$.
perOption.B: Correct. $a = r\omega^2$ with $\omega$ constant.
perOption.C: Uses $a = v^2/r$ with $v$ held constant; but at fixed period $v = 2\pi r/T$ doubles.
perOption.D: Ignores that $a$ depends on $r$ at constant $\omega$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
$M = \rho\cdot\tfrac43\pi R^3$, so $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2} = \tfrac43\pi G\rho R$.

With equal density, $g \propto R$, so $g_A : g_B = 2 : 1$.

perOption.A: Uses $g \propto 1/R^2$ with the same mass, ignoring that $M \propto R^3$.
perOption.B: Assumes $g \propto 1/R$, ignoring that mass grows with volume.
perOption.C: Correct. $g \propto \rho R$, so doubling $R$ doubles $g$.
perOption.D: Compares masses ($M \propto R^3$) and forgets to divide by $R^2$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
For a circular orbit, total energy $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ (equivalently $E = -\tfrac12 mv^2$).

$\Delta E = \dfrac{GMm}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right) = \dfrac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})(690)}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{6.5\times10^6} - \dfrac{1}{7.2\times10^6}\right) \approx +2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Check: $\tfrac12 m(7.9^2 - 7.5^2)\times10^6 \approx 2.2\times10^9\ \mathrm{J}$. Total energy increases (becomes less negative) in a higher orbit.

perOption.A: Correct. Moving to a higher orbit raises total energy by about $2\times10^9\ \mathrm{J}$.
perOption.B: This is the gain in gravitational PE alone ($\approx 4\times10^9\ \mathrm{J}$), ignoring the loss of KE.
perOption.C: This is the loss in KE alone; total energy actually increases.
perOption.D: Wrong sign and magnitude: total energy rises when moving to a higher orbit, and no combination gives this loss.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body:
Total energy equals maximum KE: $E = \tfrac12 m\omega^2 x_0^2$ with $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi(40) = 251\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

$E = \tfrac12(8.0\times10^{-3})(251)^2(5.0\times10^{-3})^2 = 6.3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J} = 6.3\ \mathrm{mJ}$.

perOption.A: Uses $f = 40$ in place of $\omega = 2\pi f$.
perOption.B: Correct. $E = \tfrac12 m(2\pi f)^2 x_0^2 = 6.3\ \mathrm{mJ}$.
perOption.C: Omits the factor $\tfrac12$ in $E = \tfrac12 m\omega^2 x_0^2$.
perOption.D: Far too large; results from a unit-conversion error with the mass or amplitude.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
Maximum amplitude is resonance, so the wave frequency equals the cork's natural frequency: $f = 1/0.12 = 8.3\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

$v = \sqrt{gd} = \sqrt{9.81\times0.30} = 1.72\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = vT = 1.72\times0.12 = 0.21\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Too small by a factor of 3; results from an arithmetic or formula error (e.g. not taking the square root properly).
perOption.B: Too small; results from using a wrong frequency (e.g. treating 0.12 s as a half-period or similar slip).
perOption.C: Correct. $\lambda = \sqrt{gd}\times T = 0.21\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.D: Too large; results from a wrong speed or frequency, e.g. not matching $f$ to the natural frequency.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
Half the frequency means double the period: the original shows two cycles across the grid, so the new wave shows one cycle.

Intensity $\propto$ amplitude$^2$, so doubling intensity multiplies amplitude by $\sqrt2 \approx 1.4$. The original amplitude is 1 grid square, so the new amplitude is about 1.4 squares, as in B.

perOption.A: Period is right but the amplitude is doubled (2 squares), which would mean $4\times$ the intensity.
perOption.B: Correct. One cycle across the grid and amplitude about $1.4$ squares.
perOption.C: Frequency has been doubled instead of halved, and amplitude doubled instead of scaled by $\sqrt2$.
perOption.D: Amplitude is about right but the frequency has been doubled instead of halved.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
The first polariser transmits half of unpolarised light: $I_1 = \tfrac12 I_o$.

Malus' law at the second: $I_2 = I_1\cos^2 60^\circ = \tfrac12 I_o\times\tfrac14 = \tfrac18 I_o$.

perOption.A: Correct. $\tfrac12 I_o\cos^2 60^\circ = \tfrac18 I_o$.
perOption.B: Uses $\cos 60^\circ$ instead of $\cos^2 60^\circ$, or forgets the first halving: $I_o\cos^2 60^\circ = \tfrac14 I_o$.
perOption.C: Uses $\sin^2 60^\circ = \tfrac34$ instead of $\cos^2 60^\circ$.
perOption.D: This is the intensity after the first polariser only.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
First minimum: $b\sin\theta = \lambda$, so for small angles the central maximum width is $\approx \dfrac{2\lambda D}{b}$.

Doubling $\lambda$ and halving $b$ multiplies the width by $2\times2 = 4$, giving $4x$.

perOption.A: Treats width as $\propto b/\lambda$ (inverted relation).
perOption.B: Assumes the two changes cancel; both actually increase the width.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two changes.
perOption.D: Correct. Width $\propto \lambda/b$, which increases by a factor of 4.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
For a grating, $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$.

Since $\sin\theta$ grows more slowly than $\theta$, $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$ (e.g. $\sin\theta_1 = 0.4$ gives $\theta_1 = 23.6^\circ$, $\theta_2 = 53.1^\circ$).

Higher orders are dimmer because the single-slit diffraction envelope falls off away from the centre.

perOption.A: Assumes $\theta \propto n$ and equal intensities; both are wrong.
perOption.B: Intensity is right, but $\theta_2 = 2\theta_1$ wrongly assumes $\theta$ (not $\sin\theta$) is proportional to $n$.
perOption.C: Angle relation is right, but the second order is dimmer, not equally bright.
perOption.D: Correct. $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$ gives $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$, and higher orders are dimmer.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
Rayleigh criterion: $\theta \approx \dfrac{\lambda}{b} = \dfrac{500\times10^{-9}}{0.35} = 1.43\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

Smallest resolvable separation on the ground: $s = h\theta = (200\times10^{3})(1.43\times10^{-6}) \approx 0.29\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Power-of-ten error, e.g. leaving the altitude in km instead of converting to m.
perOption.B: Half the correct value; for example uses $2b$ or takes half the separation.
perOption.C: Correct. $s = h\lambda/b = 0.29\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.D: Ten times too large; a power-of-ten slip in converting the altitude or wavelength.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.issues: Minor: a stray fragment (looks like part of a page number '1') appears at the bottom of the crop; question content is complete. The extracted text has option A's exponent missing ('2.9 × 10^-' ); the image shows $2.9\times10^{-4}$ m.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
The pressure in kinetic theory comes precisely from the change of momentum ($2mu$ per collision) when molecules rebound elastically from the walls.

So 'negligible change of momentum on collision with the walls' contradicts the model; the other three are standard assumptions.

perOption.A: This is a valid assumption (no intermolecular forces except during collisions).
perOption.B: This is a valid assumption (molecules treated as point particles).
perOption.C: This is a valid assumption (collisions are effectively instantaneous).
perOption.D: Correct. Each wall collision reverses the normal velocity, a momentum change of $2mu$; this is what creates pressure.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body:
For a fixed amount of gas, $\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}$ with temperatures in kelvin.

$p_2 = p_1\cdot\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\cdot\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = (1.0\times10^{5})\cdot\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{298}{323} = 4.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

perOption.A: Too small; results from compounding errors in the ratios (e.g. mishandling the temperature conversion as well as halving for the volume).
perOption.B: Uses Celsius: $(1.0\times10^5)\times\tfrac12\times\tfrac{25}{50} = 2.5\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}$.
perOption.C: Correct. $p_2 = 1.0\times10^5\times\tfrac12\times\tfrac{298}{323}$.
perOption.D: Inverts the volume ratio (multiplies by 2 instead of dividing).

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Work done on a charge in an electric field depends only on the potential difference between start and end points ($W = q\Delta V$), not on the path. Moving along an equipotential needs no work.

In the diagram all three paths start on the outer equipotential (P lies on it; Y and Z first travel along it). Y and Z end on the middle equipotential, but X ends on the innermost one, which is at a higher potential. So $W_X > W_Y = W_Z$.

The answer key gives C ($W_X = W_Y = W_Z$), which would be correct only if all three paths ended on the same equipotential.

perOption.A: Assumes longer paths need more work; work is path-independent.
perOption.B: Correct (by the diagram as printed). X ends on a higher-potential surface; Y and Z start and end on the same pair of surfaces.
perOption.C: Key's answer: true only if X also ended on the middle equipotential; as drawn, X goes further in.
perOption.D: Reverses the relationship and still treats path length as relevant.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: Answer disagreement: key says C, derived B. In the image, path X's arrowhead ends on the innermost equipotential while Y and Z end on the middle one, so W_X > W_Y = W_Z. Either the key is wrong or the diagram was drawn differently from the intended question (X ending on the middle circle would make C correct). Needs human check against the original paper/key.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body:
Electric field strength equals the negative potential gradient: $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}$.

At P, $E$ is minus the gradient of the tangent to the curve at $x = D$. Since $V$ decreases with $x$, $dV/dx$ is negative and $E$ is positive (outward).

perOption.A: $V/x$ is the gradient of the line from the origin, not the tangent, and ignores the sign; $V \ne Ex$ in a non-uniform field.
perOption.B: Uses the chord from the origin rather than the tangent gradient at P.
perOption.C: Missing the minus sign: field points in the direction of decreasing potential.
perOption.D: Correct. $E = -dV/dx$ evaluated at P.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
Charge is the area under the current–time graph, $Q = \int I\,dt$.

Steady stage: $Q_1 = 0.60 \times 3 \times 3600 = 6480\ \mathrm{C}$.

Falling stage (triangle): $Q_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.60 \times 3600 = 1080\ \mathrm{C}$.

Total $Q = 7560\ \mathrm{C} \approx 7.6 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Uses hours or minutes instead of seconds for the time.
perOption.B: Equivalent to $0.60\ \mathrm{A}$ for only 2 hours; undercounts both the 3-hour steady stage and the final hour.
perOption.D: Treats the current as $0.60\ \mathrm{A}$ for the full 4 hours instead of a triangle in the last hour.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body:
Resistance is $R = V/I$, so on an $I$–$V$ graph it is the inverse of the gradient of the line from the origin.

In D the graph is a straight line through the origin at first, so $V/I$ is constant. It then bends towards the $V$-axis, so $I$ rises less for each increase in $V$ and $R$ increases (like a filament lamp heating up).

perOption.A: $V/I$ increases from the start (curve bends over immediately); resistance is never constant.
perOption.B: Curve bends upward, so resistance decreases (diode-like), and is not initially constant.
perOption.C: Initially constant but then bends upward, so resistance decreases (thermistor-like).
perOption.D: Correct. Straight line through origin, then bends towards the $V$-axis.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
The voltmeter is across one of three identical resistors in parallel, so the p.d. across the whole parallel group is $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

The parallel group has resistance $R/3$ and is in series with $R$, so the series resistor takes 3 times the p.d.: $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

e.m.f. $= 3.0 + 9.0 = 12.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Takes the voltmeter reading as the e.m.f.; ignores the series resistor.
perOption.B: Treats the parallel group as $3R$ (adding as if in series), so the series resistor gets only $1.0\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.C: Treats the parallel group and the series resistor as having equal resistance, so equal p.d.s.
perOption.D: Correct. $R/3$ in series with $R$ gives a 1 : 3 p.d. split.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body:
$F = BIl\sin\theta = (3.4 \times 10^{-2})(3.7)(0.050)\sin 70^\circ = 5.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{N}$.

The field points to the left and the current flows down the wire (down and to the right). By Fleming's left-hand rule (or $\vec F = I\vec l \times \vec B$), the force is into the paper.

perOption.A: Uses $\cos 70^\circ$ instead of $\sin 70^\circ$; the direction is right but the magnitude is wrong.
perOption.B: Uses $\cos 70^\circ$ and the opposite direction from Fleming's left-hand rule.
perOption.C: Correct. $BIl\sin 70^\circ$, into the paper.
perOption.D: Correct magnitude but the direction is reversed (e.g. using the right hand).

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body:
1: $F = Bqv = (2.0 \times 10^{-3})(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(3.0 \times 10^{6}) = 9.6 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{N}$. Correct.

2: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the kinetic energy is unchanged. Correct.

3: Momentum is a vector. The direction turns through $90^\circ$, so $\Delta \vec p$ has magnitude $\sqrt{2}\,mv \neq 0$. Incorrect.

perOption.A: Misses that statement 2 is also correct (no work is done by a magnetic force).
perOption.B: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are true.
perOption.C: Statement 3 is false: speed is constant but the direction of momentum changes.
perOption.D: Statement 3 is false and statement 1 is true.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body:
Faraday's law: $\varepsilon = N A \dfrac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}$.

$A = \pi (0.060)^2 = 1.131 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, $\Delta B = 0.75 - 0.18 = 0.57\ \mathrm{T}$.

$\varepsilon = 5 \times 1.131 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.57 / 0.42 = 7.7 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{V} = 77\ \mathrm{mV}$.

perOption.A: Forgets the 5 turns ($15\ \mathrm{mV}$ is for one turn).
perOption.B: Does not match $NA\,\Delta B/\Delta t$; likely an arithmetic or rounding slip, as the correct value is $77\ \mathrm{mV}$.
perOption.C: Correct. $NA\,\Delta B/\Delta t = 77\ \mathrm{mV}$.
perOption.D: Too large; does not follow from the change in flux linkage $N A\,\Delta B$ over $0.42\ \mathrm{s}$ (e.g. results from using a wrong $\Delta B$ or area).

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body:
Secondary current: $I_s = V_s/R = 80/100 = 0.80\ \mathrm{A}$.

For an ideal transformer $I_p/I_s = N_s/N_p = 1000/200 = 5$, so $I_p = 5 \times 0.80 = 4.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

This is a step-up transformer: voltage goes up, so current in the primary is larger.

perOption.A: Applies the turns ratio the wrong way ($0.80/5$).
perOption.B: Gives the secondary current, not the primary current read by the ammeter.
perOption.C: Divides by $\sqrt{2}$; the meter and the $80\ \mathrm{V}$ are both r.m.s., so no conversion is needed.
perOption.D: Correct. $I_p = (N_s/N_p) I_s = 4.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body:
By the Heisenberg principle $\Delta x\,\Delta p \gtrsim h$, the smallest $\Delta p$ belongs to the electron with the largest $\Delta x$.

Wavefunction A is a sinusoid of a single wavelength spread across the whole region: its position is very uncertain, and a single $\lambda$ means a well-defined $p = h/\lambda$. So $\Delta p$ is smallest for A.

B, C and D are localised wave packets, which need a spread of wavelengths (momenta).

perOption.A: Correct. Widest spread in $x$ with a single wavelength, so smallest $\Delta p$.
perOption.B: A localised wave packet with smaller $\Delta x$, so larger $\Delta p$ than A.
perOption.C: Localised pulse; small $\Delta x$ needs a large spread of momenta.
perOption.D: Most localised packet, so it has the largest $\Delta p$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body:
An element is present only if every one of its emission lines appears in the nebula spectrum, because each element has a unique set of energy-level transitions.

All helium lines and all hydrogen lines appear in the nebula spectrum.

Nitrogen and krypton each have some lines that are missing from the nebula spectrum (some nitrogen lines near the left and one krypton line near the right), so they are not present. The extra nebula lines come from other elements.

perOption.A: Correct. Every He and H line appears in the nebula.
perOption.B: Krypton has at least one line absent from the nebula spectrum.
perOption.C: Nitrogen and krypton each have lines missing from the nebula; partial matches are not enough.
perOption.D: Ignores helium and hydrogen, whose lines all match, and wrongly includes nitrogen and krypton.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body:
In exponential decay, equal time intervals multiply the activity by the same factor.

In each 3-year period the activity falls to $\tfrac{1}{3}$, so after 6 years $A = \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 A_o = 0.11\,A_o$.

perOption.B: Halves the remaining $\tfrac{1}{3}$ (confuses with half-life), giving $\approx 0.17\,A_o$.
perOption.C: This is the activity after the first 3 years, not after another 3 years.
perOption.D: Gives the fraction that decayed in the first 3 years, not what remains.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Timing $n$ oscillations keeps the absolute uncertainty in the time (e.g. reaction time) about the same while the measured time is $n$ times longer, so the fractional uncertainty of the period $T = t/n$ falls by a factor $n$.

perOption.A: Averaging reduces the effect of random error on the mean, but the uncertainty of the diameter is still limited by the instrument's precision, so this is not the best statement.
perOption.B: A graph only reduces the effect of random error; it cannot eliminate it.
perOption.C: Correct. Fractional uncertainty in $T$ is reduced by timing many oscillations.
perOption.D: Zero error is a systematic error, not a random error.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.issues: Option A is arguably also true (averaging repeated readings reduces random error in the mean); the key relies on the convention that A's uncertainty is limited by instrument precision. Key C is the clearly correct statement.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
$R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1F_2\cos\theta$.

With $F_1 = F_2 = 1\ \mathrm{N}$, $R = 1\ \mathrm{N}$ when $\cos\theta = -\tfrac{1}{2}$, i.e. $\theta = 120^\circ$, which is between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.

For $2\ \mathrm{N}$ and $1\ \mathrm{N}$, $R = 1\ \mathrm{N}$ only at exactly $180^\circ$; for any smaller angle $R > 1\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: For $\theta < 90^\circ$, $R > \sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $\theta = 120^\circ$ gives $R = 1\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.C: For $\theta < 90^\circ$, $R > \sqrt{5}\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.D: $R = 1\ \mathrm{N}$ only at exactly $180^\circ$, which is excluded; for $90^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ$, $1 < R < \sqrt{5}\ \mathrm{N}$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
Time to fall $500\ \mathrm{m}$: $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{2(500)/9.81} = 10.1\ \mathrm{s}$.

The bomb keeps the plane's horizontal speed $138\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, while the ship moves away at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the gap closes at $126\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Release distance $= 126 \times 10.1 \approx 1270\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses a closing speed of about $100\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; no valid combination of the given speeds gives this.
perOption.B: Correct. Relative horizontal speed $126\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ times $10.1\ \mathrm{s}$.
perOption.C: Ignores the ship's motion ($138 \times 10.1$).
perOption.D: Adds the ship's speed instead of subtracting ($150 \times 10.1$).

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
In (1) the ground supports both blocks at rest: $N = (m_c + m_w)g$.

In (3) the two blocks accelerate upwards together, so $F - (m_c + m_w)g = (m_c + m_w)a$, giving $F = (m_c + m_w)(g + a) > (m_c + m_w)g$.

So the applied force in (3) exceeds the ground's force on the copper block in (1).

perOption.A: In both (1) and (2) the ground supports the total weight $(m_c + m_w)g$, so the forces are equal.
perOption.B: In (1) the wood pushes on copper with $m_w g$; in (2) copper pushes on wood with $m_c g$. These differ and are not a third-law pair.
perOption.C: In (3) the copper accelerates up, so the contact force is $m_c(g + a)$, larger than $m_c g$ in (2).
perOption.D: Correct. $F = (m_c + m_w)(g + a) > (m_c + m_w)g$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Take the ball's original direction as positive. The foot is very massive, so its velocity $v$ is unchanged.

Elastic collision: relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation: $u - v = v - 0$, using final ball velocity $0$.

So $v = u/2 = 6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the same direction as the ball (the foot moves away as the ball arrives).

perOption.A: Moving the foot towards the ball would send the ball back faster ($-36\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$), not stop it.
perOption.B: Wrong direction: ball would rebound at $-24\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Correct. $u - v = v$ gives $v = 6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ along the ball's motion.
perOption.D: Uses a mass ratio idea; the foot's mass is effectively infinite so the ratio is irrelevant.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
At constant angular speed the resultant torque is zero, so the motor torque balances the total resistive torque.

Each carriage: $85.0 \times 3.20 = 272\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. Four carriages: $4 \times 272 = 1088 \approx 1090\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.

perOption.A: Divides instead of multiplies, or slips a power of ten; the torque is $F \times r$ per carriage.
perOption.B: Counts only one carriage.
perOption.C: Counts only two carriages (as if treating the drag as couples on two arms).
perOption.D: Correct. $4 \times 85.0 \times 3.20 = 1090\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
At constant speed $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ is constant: a horizontal line.

Height falls at a constant rate, so $E_p = mgh$ decreases linearly with time. The lost $E_p$ goes to thermal energy via the viscous force, not to $E_k$.

perOption.A: $E_p$ curves (as in free fall); at constant speed $h$ decreases linearly.
perOption.B: Correct. Constant $E_k$, linearly decreasing $E_p$.
perOption.C: Describes free fall with no drag, where $E_k$ rises.
perOption.D: Assumes all lost $E_p$ becomes $E_k$; at constant speed $E_k$ cannot change.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
Old lamp light output $= 5\% \times 60 = 3.0\ \mathrm{W}$.

Modern lamp gives the same $3.0\ \mathrm{W}$ of light from $4.0\ \mathrm{W}$ input: efficiency $= 3.0/4.0 = 75\%$.

perOption.A: This is the efficiency of the old lamp.
perOption.B: Computes $4.0/60$, comparing input powers instead of useful output to input.
perOption.D: This is the old lamp's heat fraction, not an efficiency of the modern lamp.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Energy conservation from horizontal to lowest point (drop $L$): $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgL$, so $mv^2/L = 2mg$.

At P: $T - mg = mv^2/L = 2mg$, so $T = 3mg$.

perOption.A: Tension cannot be zero; it must supply centripetal force plus support the weight.
perOption.B: Ignores the centripetal force needed at P.
perOption.C: Gives the centripetal force $mv^2/L$ only, forgetting to add $mg$.
perOption.D: Correct. $T = mg + 2mg = 3mg$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body:
Field (vector): from P, $Gm/d^2$ towards P; from Q, $G(2m)/(2d)^2 = Gm/(2d^2)$ towards Q. Net $= Gm/d^2 - Gm/(2d^2) = Gm/(2d^2)$ towards P.

Potential (scalar, always negative): $\phi = -\dfrac{Gm}{d} - \dfrac{G(2m)}{2d} = -2\dfrac{Gm}{d}$.

perOption.A: Wrongly assumes the fields cancel and uses only one potential term.
perOption.B: Correct potential but takes only P's field, ignoring Q's opposing field.
perOption.C: Assumes the fields cancel and adds the potentials wrongly.
perOption.D: Correct. Net field $Gm/(2d^2)$, potential $-2Gm/d$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
The compression is sudden and the cylinder is insulating, so $Q = 0$. The piston does work on the gas, so by $\Delta U = Q + W$ the internal energy, and hence the temperature, rises.

Microscopically, molecules striking the inward-moving piston rebound with greater speed, raising their mean kinetic energy, which is proportional to $T$.

perOption.A: An insulator stops heat flow ($Q = 0$), but work is still done on the gas, so $U$ and $T$ rise.
perOption.B: $pV$ is constant only for an isothermal change; here $pV = NkT$ increases because $T$ increases.
perOption.C: Collisions between molecules are elastic and do not change the total kinetic energy, so they cannot raise the temperature.
perOption.D: Correct. Molecules gain speed from the moving piston, so mean KE and $T$ increase.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
For a closed cycle the net work equals the enclosed area: $\Delta p \times \Delta V = (0.5\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa})(3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}) = 15\ \mathrm{J}$.

The cycle runs clockwise: the gas expands at the higher pressure ($1.5\times10^5$ Pa) and is compressed at the lower pressure, so the gas does net work of 15 J. The net work done on the gas is therefore $-15\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Wrong power of ten and wrong sign: the area is 15 J, and it is work done by the gas.
perOption.B: Correct sign but the area is miscalculated by a factor of 10 ($0.5\times10^5 \times 3\times10^{-4} = 15$ J).
perOption.C: This is the work done by the gas; the work done on the gas is negative for a clockwise cycle.
perOption.D: Correct. Clockwise cycle, so net work on the gas is minus the enclosed area.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
In SHM $v = \omega\sqrt{x_0^2 - x^2}$ and $v_0 = \omega x_0$.

With $x = \tfrac{1}{2}x_0$: $v = \omega\sqrt{x_0^2 - \tfrac{1}{4}x_0^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\omega x_0 = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}v_0$.

perOption.A: No step in the SHM relations gives a factor of $\tfrac{1}{4}$; speed is not $v_0$ times $(x/x_0)^2$.
perOption.B: Assumes speed falls linearly with displacement, which it does not.
perOption.C: This is the fraction of the maximum kinetic energy ($v^2/v_0^2 = 3/4$), not of the speed; forgets the square root.
perOption.D: Correct. $v = \omega\sqrt{x_0^2 - x_0^2/4} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}v_0$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
P is at the centre of a compression (lines crowded together) and Q is at the centre of a rarefaction (lines spread apart).

In a progressive longitudinal wave, the particles at the centre of a compression or rarefaction have zero displacement and are moving at maximum speed. At a compression they move in the direction of travel of the wave, so the molecule at P moves in the $+x$ direction.

perOption.A: P is at a compression, so the pressure there is a maximum, not a minimum.
perOption.B: Nodes and antinodes belong to stationary waves; this is a progressive wave.
perOption.C: At the centre of a rarefaction the displacement is zero and the speed is maximum (moving in $-x$), not zero.
perOption.D: Correct. At a compression the particles move in the direction the wave travels.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
Open at both ends: $f_n = n\dfrac{v}{2L}$, so the fundamental is $\dfrac{v}{2L} = 256\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

Closed at one end: $f = (2n-1)\dfrac{v}{4L}$, so only odd harmonics of $\dfrac{v}{4L} = 128\ \mathrm{Hz}$ exist. The two lowest are $128\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $3 \times 128 = 384\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Includes the second harmonic (256 Hz), but a tube closed at one end has only odd harmonics.
perOption.B: Correct. Fundamental halves to 128 Hz; next mode is the third harmonic, 384 Hz.
perOption.C: Skips the fundamental and uses 3rd and 5th harmonics only.
perOption.D: Doubles the frequencies instead of halving them; closing an end lengthens the fundamental wavelength.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
From $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$: $d\sin 45^\circ = 3\lambda$, so $\dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3}{\sin 45^\circ} = 4.24$.

The largest order satisfies $\sin\theta \le 1$, i.e. $n \le d/\lambda = 4.24$, so the highest order is the 4th.

perOption.A: The 3rd order is at only 45°, so higher orders still fit before 90°.
perOption.B: Correct. $n_{max} = \lfloor 3/\sin45^\circ \rfloor = 4$.
perOption.C: Rounds 4.24 up; a 5th order would need $\sin\theta > 1$.
perOption.D: Doubles the 3rd order, assuming orders scale linearly with angle (45° to 90°).

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
Charge passing: $Q = It = (20\times10^{-3})(5.0) = 0.10\ \mathrm{C}$.

Number of electrons: $N = \dfrac{Q}{e} = \dfrac{0.10}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 6.3\times10^{17}$.

perOption.A: This is the charge in coulombs, not the number of electrons.
perOption.B: Far too small to be an electron count; it comes from mishandling units rather than dividing the charge by $e$.
perOption.C: Correct. $N = It/e$.
perOption.D: Does not equal $It/e$; results from mishandling the powers of ten when converting mA or dividing by $e$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body:
The e.m.f. is the same in both cases: $E = I(R + r)$.

$1.00(3.0 + r) = 0.40(12.0 + r) \Rightarrow 3.0 + r = 4.8 + 0.4r \Rightarrow 0.6r = 1.8 \Rightarrow r = 3.0\ \Omega$ (and $E = 6.0$ V).

perOption.A: Comes from an algebra slip in the simultaneous equations; substituting back gives different e.m.f.s.
perOption.B: Correct. Equating $E = I(R+r)$ for both readings gives $r = 3.0\ \Omega$.
perOption.C: This is $E$ in volts (6.0 V), not $r$.
perOption.D: Arithmetic slip; with $r = 13\ \Omega$ the two readings would give different e.m.f.s.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Each capacitor has capacitance $C$. The lower branch (two in series) is $C/2$; in parallel with the upper capacitor this gives $1.5C$.

X is in series with this $1.5C$ combination, so the combination also holds $6\ \mu\mathrm{C}$. Parallel branches share the same p.d., so charge divides in proportion to capacitance: upper $C$ gets $4\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and the lower $C/2$ branch gets $2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

Capacitors in series carry the same charge, so Y holds $2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The $C/2$ branch takes one-third of the $6\ \mu$C.
perOption.B: Splits the charge equally between the two parallel branches.
perOption.C: This is the charge on the single upper capacitor, not on Y.
perOption.D: Assumes every capacitor carries the same charge as X.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body:
$E = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$ and $V = V_0 e^{-t/RC}$, so $E = E_0 e^{-2t/RC}$.

Setting $E = E_0/8$: $e^{-2t/RC} = \tfrac{1}{8} \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{RC\ln 8}{2}$. With $RC = (2200\times10^{-6})(4.7\times10^{3}) = 10.3\ \mathrm{s}$, $t = \dfrac{10.3 \times 2.08}{2} \approx 11\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Energy decays twice as fast as voltage: $t = \tfrac{1}{2}RC\ln 8$.
perOption.B: Does not follow from $E = E_0e^{-2t/RC}$; arises from mixing up the decay constant for energy with that for charge.
perOption.C: Uses $t = RC\ln 8$, treating energy as decaying like $V$ or $Q$ and forgetting $E \propto V^2$.
perOption.D: Uses $t = 3RC$, confusing three halvings with three time constants (and ignoring $E \propto V^2$).

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
In every arrangement the net force is zero, since the charges sum to zero: $(+2Q + Q - 2Q - Q)E = 0$. Equilibrium also needs zero resultant torque.

In B, the left side has $+2Q$ (top) and $-Q$ (bottom), and the right side has $-2Q$ (top) and $+Q$ (bottom). Top row: $+2Q$ is pushed right and $-2Q$ is pushed left, both acting along the same line, so they cancel. Bottom row: $-Q$ is pushed left and $+Q$ is pushed right, also along one line. No couple acts, so the square is in equilibrium.

In A, C and D the forces on the charges do not share lines of action, so they form a net couple and the square rotates.

perOption.A: Rightward forces ($2QE$ at top right, $QE$ at bottom right) and leftward forces at the left corners act on different lines, so a net couple remains.
perOption.B: Correct. Equal and opposite forces in each row act along the same line, so there is no couple (the equilibrium is unstable).
perOption.C: The $+2Q$ and $+Q$ forces are horizontal but $-2Q$ and $-Q$ sit at the top and bottom, giving a net torque.
perOption.D: The top row is pushed right ($3QE$) and the bottom row left ($3QE$), forming a couple.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.issues: Question number is cut off in the crop (Q21 by id). The equilibrium in the key's answer B is unstable; the question does not ask about stability, so the key stands.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body:
P is positive and balanced, so the electric force is upward: the field points up and the lower plate is at the higher potential.

When $V$ is decreased, P falls. Its gravitational PE decreases. It moves towards the higher-potential lower plate, so its electric PE ($qV$) increases.

perOption.A: Moving a positive charge towards higher potential increases its electric PE.
perOption.B: Correct. Falling lowers GPE, and moving towards the higher-potential plate raises EPE.
perOption.C: When P rises, it moves towards lower potential, so its electric PE decreases even though GPE increases.
perOption.D: The changes are equal only if no kinetic energy is gained; P accelerates, so this need not hold.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
The electric field points out of the page (towards D). Electrons feel an electric force opposite to $E$, i.e. into the page (towards B).

For no deflection, the magnetic force must point out of the page (towards D). Conventional current is opposite to the electron motion, i.e. to the left. By Fleming's left-hand rule, a leftward current with a force out of the page needs $B$ pointing downward, towards C. (Check: $\vec F = -e\,\vec v \times \vec B$ with $\vec v$ to the right and $\vec B$ downward gives a force out of the page.)

perOption.A: Gives a magnetic force into the page, adding to the electric force instead of cancelling it; this is the answer for positive charges.
perOption.B: B parallel to the electric force direction; the magnetic force would then be vertical and could not cancel the electric force.
perOption.C: Correct. Downward B gives an out-of-page magnetic force on the electrons, balancing the electric force.
perOption.D: B along $E$ gives a vertical magnetic force, which cannot balance the electric force.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body:
Reversing the pole reverses the change in flux linkage, so by Lenz's law the induced current, and the needle deflection, reverse: to the right.

At half the speed the rate of change of flux linkage is smaller, so by Faraday's law the induced e.m.f. and maximum current are smaller: less than 10 units.

perOption.A: Ignores the reversal of direction caused by using the South pole.
perOption.B: Correct. Opposite pole reverses the direction; slower motion reduces the e.m.f.
perOption.C: Wrong direction, and a slower speed gives a smaller, not larger, e.m.f.
perOption.D: Direction is right, but half the speed reduces the rate of change of flux, so the deflection is smaller.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body:
With the disc turning anticlockwise, the radius PQ (P at the top) moves to the left. With $B$ into the page, the magnetic force on positive charges, $q\vec v\times\vec B$, points down along the radius towards Q.

So current flows from P to Q inside the disc. The disc acts as the source, so charge is driven to Q, making Q the positive terminal. P is at a lower potential than Q, and the external current flows from Q through the resistor back to P.

perOption.A: Correct. The force on positive charges is towards Q, so Q is the higher-potential terminal.
perOption.B: Reverses the current direction in the radius.
perOption.C: Reverses both: this would be correct for clockwise rotation.
perOption.D: Assumes current in the source flows from high to low potential; inside the e.m.f. source it flows from low to high.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body:
One period is 4 s: $I = 4.0$ A for 1 s, $I = -2.0$ A for 2 s (1 s to 3 s), then $I = 0$ for 1 s.

Energy per period: $W = R\sum I^2 t = 11(16\times1 + 4\times2 + 0) = 264\ \mathrm{J}$. Average power $= 264/4 = 66\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Zero is the mean current (net charge per cycle is zero), but power depends on $I^2$, which is never negative.
perOption.B: Leaves out part of the period, e.g. uses only the positive pulse ($16\times11/4 = 44$ W).
perOption.C: Correct. Mean of $I^2R$ over the 4 s period.
perOption.D: Overestimates the mean of $I^2$, e.g. by taking the 4.0 A pulse to last half of each period.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The de Broglie relation is $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$, so $\lambda p = h$, a constant. Wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum.

perOption.A: Correct. $\lambda p = h$.
perOption.B: Inverts the relationship: wavelength decreases as momentum increases.
perOption.C: Since $p = \sqrt{2mE_k}$, $\lambda\sqrt{E_k}$ is constant, not $\lambda E_k$.
perOption.D: Wavelength decreases with kinetic energy, so this ratio cannot be constant.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body:
$|\psi|^2$ gives the probability density of finding the particle at $x$, so its spread measures the position uncertainty $\Delta x$.

By $\Delta x\,\Delta p \gtrsim h$, the smallest $\Delta x$ gives the largest $\Delta p$. Graph D is the most sharply localised, so it has the largest momentum uncertainty.

perOption.A: A uniform $|\psi|^2$ means maximum $\Delta x$, so the smallest $\Delta p$.
perOption.B: The particle is spread over the whole range, so $\Delta x$ is large and $\Delta p$ small.
perOption.C: A broad single hump spans the whole region, so $\Delta x$ is large.
perOption.D: Correct. The narrowest distribution gives the smallest $\Delta x$ and so the largest $\Delta p$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: Question number is cut off in the crop (Q28 by id).

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body:
Change in neutron number: $\beta^-$ decay turns a neutron into a proton ($-1$); $\alpha$ decay removes 2 neutrons ($-2$); $\gamma$ emission changes nothing (0).

Totals: A $-1$, B $-2$, C $-3$, D $-2$. Sequence A loses the fewest neutrons.

perOption.A: Correct. Only one neutron is lost (β), and γ emission leaves the nucleus composition unchanged.
perOption.B: α emission removes 2 neutrons.
perOption.C: Loses 2 (α) + 1 (β) = 3 neutrons, the most.
perOption.D: Each β decay converts a neutron into a proton, so 2 neutrons are lost.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body:
Let the source rate be $S$ and the background $b$. Then $S + b = 324$, and after two half-lives $\tfrac{S}{4} + b = 108$.

Subtracting: $\tfrac{3}{4}S = 216 \Rightarrow S = 288$, so $b = 324 - 288 = 36$ counts per minute.

perOption.A: This is $108/4$, which wrongly treats the background as decaying too.
perOption.B: Correct. Only the source count decays; the background stays constant.
perOption.C: This is $108/2$, which wrongly halves the final reading.
perOption.D: This is $S/4$ (the remaining source count), not the background.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
For $x = \dfrac{ab^2}{c}$, percentage uncertainties add, with each multiplied by its power: $\dfrac{\Delta x}{x} = \dfrac{\Delta a}{a} + 2\dfrac{\Delta b}{b} + \dfrac{\Delta c}{c}$.

For A: $4 + 2(2) + 4 = 12\%$.

perOption.B: Gives $2 + 2(8) + 2 = 20\%$; it only totals 12% if the power of 2 on $b$ is ignored.
perOption.C: Gives $3 + 2(2) + 2 = 9\%$; it totals 7% if the power is ignored, so neither way gives 12%.
perOption.D: Gives $6 + 2(2) + 4 = 14\%$; it only totals 12% if the power of 2 on $b$ is ignored.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
Velocity of P relative to Q is $\vec v_P - \vec v_Q = \vec v_P + (-\vec v_Q)$.

That is $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ north plus $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ west, giving a vector pointing mostly north and slightly west, which is arrow D.

perOption.A: Points south-east, which matches neither the north 3.0 nor the west 1.0 component of $\vec v_P - \vec v_Q$.
perOption.B: Points north-west at about 45°, which would need equal north and west components rather than 3 : 1.
perOption.C: Points mostly south and slightly east, which is $\vec v_Q - \vec v_P$ (Q relative to P), the reverse vector.
perOption.D: Correct. Mostly north (3.0) with a small westward part (1.0).

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
Treat the sheet as a full square minus the hole. Full square: area $16\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, centre $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ below M. Hole: area $2.0\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, centre $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ above the bottom, i.e. $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ below M.

$y = \dfrac{16(2.0) - 2.0(3.0)}{16 - 2.0} = \dfrac{26}{14} = 1.9\ \mathrm{cm}$ below M.

Removing material below the centre moves the centre of gravity up, towards M.

perOption.A: Too far upward; the small hole only shifts the centre by about $0.14\ \mathrm{cm}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $26/14 \approx 1.9\ \mathrm{cm}$.
perOption.C: Adds the hole instead of subtracting it: $(32 + 6)/18 = 2.1\ \mathrm{cm}$; removing mass below the centre must raise the centre of gravity.
perOption.D: Lies below the full square's centre, which is impossible when material below the centre is removed.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Only the lowest side is in the vertical field; the current along it is horizontal, so the magnetic force $F = NBIL$ is horizontal.

Take moments about the pivot (top side), side $L$: weight acts at the centre, perpendicular distance $\tfrac{L}{2}\sin 30^\circ$; horizontal force acts at the bottom, perpendicular distance $L\cos 30^\circ$.

$0.30 \times \tfrac{L}{2}\sin 30^\circ = F L\cos 30^\circ \Rightarrow F = 0.15\tan 30^\circ = 0.0866\ \mathrm{N}$.

$B = \dfrac{F}{NIL} = \dfrac{0.0866}{100(0.40)(0.050)} = 0.043\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Takes the perpendicular distance of the magnetic force as $L$ instead of $L\cos 30^\circ$, giving $F = 0.075\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.C: Puts the weight at the bottom side and takes the force's distance as $L$, giving $F = 0.30\sin 30^\circ = 0.15\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.D: Takes the weight to act at the bottom side ($F = 0.30\tan 30^\circ$), ignoring that it acts at the centre of the coil.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
While the constant force acts, $a = F/m$ is constant, so velocity rises linearly from zero.

When the force stops, there is no friction, so by Newton's first law the body keeps a constant velocity.

perOption.A: Velocity copies the force graph, as if $v \propto F$; velocity cannot jump instantly.
perOption.B: Correct. Linear rise during the force, then constant velocity.
perOption.C: Shows the body slowing to rest after the force stops, which needs a resistive force; the table is frictionless.
perOption.D: Curved rise implies increasing acceleration, but a constant force gives constant acceleration.

perOption.A: Half the correct tension; the resultant force on the cart must be $ma = 90\ \mathrm{N}$ on top of the 40 N resistance.
perOption.B: Too small: it does not satisfy $T - 40 = 90\ \mathrm{N}$, e.g. from an arithmetic slip with $ma$.
perOption.C: Correct. $T = 40 + 90 = 130\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.D: 1.5 times the correct value; the tension only needs to supply $ma$ plus the 40 N resistance.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
Useful power: $P = Fv = 1600 \times 11 = 1.76 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{W}$.

Input power: $\dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{6}}{60} = 3.0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{W}$.

Efficiency $= \dfrac{1.76 \times 10^4}{3.0 \times 10^4} = 59\%$.

perOption.A: Too low: useful power is $Fv = 17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$, which is well over a fifth of the 30 kW input.
perOption.B: Too low: does not equal $Fv$ divided by the fuel power $1.8\ \mathrm{MJ}/60\ \mathrm{s}$.
perOption.C: Too low: does not equal $Fv$ divided by the fuel power, e.g. from mis-converting minutes or kN.
perOption.D: Correct. $17.6\ \mathrm{kW} / 30\ \mathrm{kW} = 59\%$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
Total energy is constant, so KE + GPE is always equal to the initial KE.

At the top the ball still moves horizontally at $u\cos 60^\circ = u/2$, so KE there is $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of the initial value and GPE is $\tfrac{3}{4}$.

So KE dips to about a quarter (not zero) and GPE peaks at about three quarters, with the curves crossing: graph D.

perOption.A: Shows KE falling to zero at the top, which only happens for a vertical launch.
perOption.B: Shows KE and GPE equal at the top, which is a 45° launch ($\cos^2 45^\circ = \tfrac12$).
perOption.C: Shows KE staying large and GPE small at the top, which fits a low launch angle, not 60°.
perOption.D: Correct. Minimum KE is $\cos^2 60^\circ = \tfrac14$ of the initial KE.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
For an elastic collision, relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation: $v - 0 = 0.4v - v_P$.

So $v_P = -0.6v$: P rebounds to the left with speed $0.6v$ (Q must be 4 times as massive as P, consistent with momentum).

perOption.A: Only for equal masses does P stop, but then Q would move off with $v$, not $0.4v$.
perOption.B: Assumes P moves at the same speed as Q, which would make the relative speed of separation zero or $0.8v$.
perOption.C: Correct. $v_P = 0.4v - v = -0.6v$.
perOption.D: Would require no change in P's speed, which violates energy conservation once Q gains KE.

perOption.A: Far too small; results from a wrong factor of $2\pi$ or $T$ in $\omega$.
perOption.B: This is the speed $v = r\omega \approx 0.205\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, not the acceleration.
perOption.C: Too small; results from a wrong factor in $\omega$, e.g. not squaring it correctly.
perOption.D: Correct. $a = 4\pi^2 r/T^2 = 0.546\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
Gravitational field strength is the negative potential gradient: $g = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dr}$.

So the field is perpendicular to the equipotentials and points towards decreasing potential, i.e. towards the $-500\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ line. That is arrow A.

perOption.A: Correct. Perpendicular to the equipotentials, towards more negative potential.
perOption.B: Lies along an equipotential; no work is done moving along it, so there is no field component in this direction.
perOption.C: Points towards higher potential ($-200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$), the opposite of the field direction.
perOption.D: Lies along an equipotential, so the field has no component along it.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
For a point mass, $\phi = -\dfrac{GM}{r}$, so $|\phi| \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$. Doubling the distance halves it: $\phi/2$.

The potential difference between P and Q is $GM\left(\dfrac{1}{r_P} - \dfrac{1}{r_Q}\right)$. Further out the field is weaker, so the same separation gives a smaller potential difference.

perOption.A: The magnitude at 2x is exactly $\phi/2$, not less, since $|\phi| \propto 1/r$.
perOption.B: Wrong on both counts: magnitude is exactly $\phi/2$, and the p.d. decreases because the field is weaker.
perOption.C: Correct. $|\phi| \propto 1/r$ and the potential gradient is smaller further out.
perOption.D: Treats the field as uniform; in a radial field the p.d. across a fixed gap falls with distance.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
The acceleration graph completes one cycle in 2 s, so $T = 2\ \mathrm{s}$. At $t = 0$, $a = 0$, so $x = 0$ (since $a = -\omega^2 x$) and the speed is maximum.

KE is maximum whenever the particle passes equilibrium, which happens twice per cycle: at $t = 0, 1, 2\ \mathrm{s}$. So KE has period 1 s and starts at its maximum: graph C.

perOption.A: Has the right starting value but only one KE cycle in 2 s; KE has half the period of the motion.
perOption.B: Starts at zero KE and has only one cycle, wrong in both phase and period.
perOption.C: Correct. KE maximum at $t = 0$, 1 s and 2 s.
perOption.D: Has the right period but starts at zero KE, which corresponds to maximum displacement, not $a = 0$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
The front of the pulse must travel $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ to O and $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ back to P: $0.75\ \mathrm{m}$ at $0.50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ takes 1.5 s. The 0.25 m pulse takes 0.5 s to pass, so the reflected pulse passes P from 1.5 s to 2.0 s.

At the fixed end the pulse is inverted. The front of the incident pulse is the large trough, so the reflected pulse reaches P first as a large crest, followed by a small trough: graph D.

perOption.A: This is the incident pulse passing P (small crest then large trough), which happens from 0.5 s to 1.0 s.
perOption.B: Shows the incident pulse inverted but in the wrong time order: the large part (the front) must reach P first.
perOption.C: Shows the original pulse in reverse order without inversion; reflection at a fixed end inverts the pulse.
perOption.D: Correct. Inverted reflected pulse: large crest first, then small trough.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
Power received $\propto$ intensity $= \dfrac{P_{\text{source}}}{4\pi r^2}$ for a fixed surface area.

Doubling the source power ×2, doubling distance ×$\tfrac14$: $1.4 \times 2 \times \tfrac14 = 0.70\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Applies the inverse-square factor but forgets to double the source power.
perOption.B: Correct. $1.4 \times 2/4 = 0.70\ \mathrm{W}$.
perOption.C: Uses $I \propto 1/r$, so the two factors of 2 cancel.
perOption.D: Doubles for the source power but ignores the distance change.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
The two third-order lines are symmetric about the normal, so each is at $\theta = 30^\circ$.

$d\sin\theta = n\lambda \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{3(500 \times 10^{-9})}{\sin 30^\circ} = 3.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$.

Lines per mm $= \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-3}}{3.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 333$.

perOption.A: Correct. $d = 3.0\ \mathrm{\mu m}$, so 333 lines per mm.
perOption.B: Does not follow from $d\sin 30^\circ = 3\lambda$; arises from using a wrong angle for $\theta$.
perOption.C: Double the correct value; omits the $\sin 30^\circ$ factor, i.e. takes $d = 3\lambda$.
perOption.D: Gives lines per metre, not per millimetre.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
By the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta \approx \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$.

With visible light $\lambda \approx 500\ \mathrm{nm}$: $\theta \approx \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-7}}{2.4} \approx 2 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Too small by a factor of about 20; would need a wavelength in the X-ray region.
perOption.B: Correct. $\lambda/b \approx 2 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{rad}$.
perOption.C: About 50 times too large; corresponds to a wavelength of about 24 µm (infrared), or a much smaller aperture.
perOption.D: About 100 times too large; corresponds to a far-infrared wavelength or a mis-converted unit.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body:
Using $\Delta U = Q + W$ where $W$ is work done on the gas: along ACB, $\Delta U = 16 + (-6) = 10\ \mathrm{J}$.

Internal energy depends only on the state, so $\Delta U = 10\ \mathrm{J}$ along ADB too: $10 = Q + (-2) \Rightarrow Q = 12\ \mathrm{J}$ into the gas.

perOption.A: Uses $Q = \Delta U - \ldots$ with the wrong sign, e.g. treats work done by the gas as positive work done on it.
perOption.B: Correct. $Q = \Delta U + W_{\text{by}} = 10 + 2 = 12\ \mathrm{J}$ in.
perOption.C: Assumes heat transfer is path-independent; only $\Delta U$ is a state function.
perOption.D: Adds the work the wrong way: $16 + 6 - 2 = 20$, mixing up sign conventions.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water, and $c$ and density cancel: $120(60 - T) = 30(T - 20)$.

$7200 - 120T = 30T - 600 \Rightarrow T = 52\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Far too close to the cold temperature; weights the cold water much too heavily.
perOption.B: Swaps the masses, pairing 30 cm³ with 60 °C and 120 cm³ with 20 °C.
perOption.C: Uses the simple average of the two temperatures, ignoring the different amounts of water.
perOption.D: Correct. Weighted mean $(120 \times 60 + 30 \times 20)/150 = 52\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body:
$E \propto \dfrac{Q}{r^2}$. Compared with $+2q$ at 0.30 m, $-q$ at 0.60 m has half the charge and twice the distance: $E = 24 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{4} = 3\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

At P the field of $+2q$ points away from it (towards $-q$), and the field of $-q$ points towards $-q$. Both act in the same direction, so $E = 24 + 3 = 27\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses $E \propto 1/r$ (giving $6\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ from $-q$) and subtracts it.
perOption.B: Subtracts the fields ($24 - 3$), not noticing that both point towards $-q$ between the charges.
perOption.C: Correct. Fields add: $24 + 3 = 27\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: Uses $1/r$ instead of $1/r^2$, giving $6\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ from $-q$, then adds.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
In series the current is the same, so $nAv$ is the same in both wires: $n_X A_X v_X = n_Y A_Y v_Y$.

$n_X = 2n_Y$ and $A_X = \tfrac{1}{4}A_Y$ (area $\propto d^2$), so $n_X A_X = \tfrac{1}{2} n_Y A_Y$.

Hence $v_Y = \tfrac{1}{2} v_X = 0.26\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $v_Y = v_X/2$.
perOption.B: Takes area proportional to diameter (not $d^2$), so $nA$ is the same in both wires.
perOption.C: Inverts the ratio, giving $v_Y = 2v_X$ instead of $v_X/2$.
perOption.D: Uses only the area ratio and inverts it, giving $4v_X$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body:
The supply p.d. is shared between the NTC–LDR pair and the fixed resistor in proportion to resistance.

The voltmeter reading is largest when the NTC and LDR have the largest resistance. An NTC thermistor has high resistance at low temperature, and an LDR has high resistance in dim light. So low temperature and low brightness.

perOption.A: High temperature and high brightness both make the resistances smallest, giving the smallest reading.
perOption.B: High temperature lowers the NTC resistance.
perOption.C: High brightness lowers the LDR resistance.
perOption.D: Correct. Both resistances are maximised.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
The two $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors are in parallel, giving $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. This is in series with the two $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors.

Three $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ in series: $\frac{1}{C} = \frac{3}{4}$, so $C = \tfrac{4}{3}\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

Charge circulated $Q = CV = \tfrac{4}{3} \times 12 = 16\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $Q = \tfrac{4}{3}\ \mu\mathrm{F} \times 12\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.B: Uses $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ effective capacitance (e.g. only two $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ in series).
perOption.C: Uses $3\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, a wrong series/parallel combination.
perOption.D: Uses far too large an effective capacitance, as if capacitors were combined in parallel.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body:
Peak current $I_0 = \sqrt{2}I$, so peak power $P_0 = I_0^2 R = 2I^2 \times 2.0 = 4I^2$.

$P = I_0^2 R \sin^2 \omega t$ is always positive and touches zero smoothly (a $\sin^2$ curve), oscillating at twice the current frequency. Graph D has this shape and peak $4I^2$.

perOption.A: Shape is $|\sin|$ (sharp cusps at zero) and the peak value is wrong.
perOption.B: Peak $\sqrt{2}I^2$ is wrong: uses $\sqrt{2}I$ without squaring and ignores $R$.
perOption.C: Peak $2I^2$ uses the r.m.s. current $I^2R$, which is the mean power, not the peak.
perOption.D: Correct. Peak $= (\sqrt{2}I)^2(2.0) = 4I^2$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body:
The electron travels upward. For a straight path, any force perpendicular to the motion must cancel; forces along the motion only change speed.

In B, $E$ is into the page, so the electric force is along the page normal, while the magnetic force ($\vec v \times \vec B$ with $B$ out of page) lies in the page plane, sideways. These perpendicular forces cannot cancel, so the electron must deflect.

In A, $B$ is parallel to $v$ (no magnetic force) and the electric force is along the motion. In C and D, a component of the electric force can balance the magnetic force.

perOption.A: $B$ parallel to $v$ gives zero magnetic force and $E$ only acts along the path, so it is possible.
perOption.B: Correct. Electric force is out of the page plane, magnetic force is sideways in the plane; they cannot cancel.
perOption.C: Electric force has a horizontal component that can cancel the sideways magnetic force; the vertical component just changes speed.
perOption.D: Magnetic force on the electron is out of the page and the electric force is into the page, so they can cancel.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body:
Area swept $= Lvt = 0.24 \times 0.50 \times 30 = 3.6\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

Flux cut $\Phi = BA = 0.15 \times 3.6 = 0.54\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

perOption.A: Gives the flux cut per second ($BLv$), not in 30 s.
perOption.B: Uses a wrong time or doubles the per-second value instead of using 30 s.
perOption.C: Correct. $\Phi = BLvt$.
perOption.D: Uses 60 s (a full minute) instead of 30 s.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body:
Same frequency means each photon has the same energy $E = hf$.

Intensity is power per unit area, so a greater intensity means more photons cross unit area per unit time.

perOption.A: Same frequency means each photon has the same energy $hf$.
perOption.B: All photons travel at $c$ in a given medium.
perOption.C: Amplitude is a wave description, not a particle (photon) explanation.
perOption.D: Correct. Higher photon flux per unit area.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body:
The slit fixes the electron's transverse position to within the slit width, so $\Delta y$ is defined at the slit, across it.

The resulting uncertainty in momentum is in the same transverse direction ($y$), also at the slit, and this spread causes the diffraction pattern on the screen.

perOption.A: Correct. Both $\Delta y$ and $\Delta p$ are transverse and at the slit.
perOption.B: $\Delta y$ and $\Delta p$ are defined where the electron passes through the slit, not at the screen.
perOption.C: $\Delta p$ must be in the same ($y$) direction as $\Delta y$, not along the direction of travel.
perOption.D: $\Delta y$ is at the slit, and $\Delta p$ must be transverse.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body:
X has proton number 94 and neutron number 145.

In $\beta^-$ decay a neutron becomes a proton: proton number rises by 1, neutron number falls by 1. The daughter is at (95, 144), which is nuclide B.

perOption.A: (92, 141) needs loss of 2 protons and 4 neutrons, not a single beta decay.
perOption.B: Correct. $Z+1$, $N-1$.
perOption.C: (93, 145) lowers the proton number with no neutron change; $\beta^-$ decay raises $Z$.
perOption.D: (95, 145) increases $Z$ without decreasing $N$, ignoring that a neutron is converted.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body:
Large-angle deflections (up to $180^\circ$) need a very strong repulsive force from a small, massive, positively charged region: the nucleus.

Most α-particles pass far from nuclei and are hardly deflected; the few that come close are strongly repelled.

perOption.A: α-particles in this experiment have de Broglie wavelengths far too small for lattice diffraction to give such angles.
perOption.B: The foil is very thin and most particles pass straight through; surface reflection does not occur.
perOption.C: Electrons are far too light to deflect a massive α-particle significantly.
perOption.D: Correct. Coulomb repulsion by small, dense, positive nuclei.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
For $\frac{3PQ^4}{R^2}$: total % uncertainty $= \%P + 4(\%Q) + 2(\%R)$; the constant 3 contributes nothing.

C: $3.0 + 4(1.0) + 2(2.0) = 11\%$.

perOption.D: Gives $5 + 8 + 2 = 15\%$; simple addition without powers gives 8%.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
Y's graph is X's graph shifted down by $v/4$, so Y's displacement is less than X's by $\tfrac{v}{4}t_2$: displacements differ.

X has velocity $\ge 0$ throughout, so its distance $= \tfrac{1}{2}vt_2$. Y has negative velocity for part of the time; its distance (sum of magnitudes of areas) works out to $\tfrac{5}{16}vt_2$, so the distances also differ.

perOption.A: Correct. Both displacement and distance differ.
perOption.B: Distance is not the same: the downward shift reduces positive area by more than the small negative area adds.
perOption.C: Displacement differs because Y's graph is shifted down by $v/4$.
perOption.D: Same shape does not mean same area; both quantities change.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
Elastic potential energy is the area under the force–extension graph.

At extension $x$ the stored energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}Fx$, so the change from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}(F_2x_2 - F_1x_1)$ (the trapezium area).

perOption.A: Omits the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ for the triangular area.
perOption.B: Correct. Difference of two triangle areas.
perOption.C: Squares the extensions; dimensionally $Fx^2$ is not energy.
perOption.D: Squares the extensions, confusing $\tfrac{1}{2}Fx$ with $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Forces on the lift: $T$ up, $W_2$ and $D$ down. If $T = D + W_2$, the resultant force on the lift is zero, so by Newton's first law it moves with constant velocity (which includes being at rest).

The other statements fail when the lift accelerates, or confuse "no resultant force" with "at rest".

perOption.A: Only true when the lift is not accelerating; when accelerating $T \ne W_1 + W_2$.
perOption.B: $N = W_1$ only means zero acceleration; the lift could move at constant velocity.
perOption.C: $N$ and $W_1$ are not a Newton's third law pair; they differ when the lift accelerates.
perOption.D: Correct. Zero resultant force on the lift means constant velocity.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Down a frictionless slope the accelerating force is $mg\sin\theta$, so $a = g\sin\theta$, independent of mass.

Doubling the mass doubles the accelerating force but leaves the acceleration as $a$.

perOption.A: The accelerating force $mg\sin\theta$ doubles with mass.
perOption.B: Assumes the force stays the same while mass doubles.
perOption.C: Correct. $a = g\sin\theta$.
perOption.D: Assumes force doubles without accounting for doubled mass.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
Whole system: $a = \frac{54 - 6.0}{8.0} = 6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

The friction is drawn acting on the 6.0 kg block, so the only horizontal force on the 2.0 kg block is the push from the 6.0 kg block: $F = ma = 2.0 \times 6.0 = 12\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $F = 2.0 \times 6.0$.
perOption.B: Gives the net force on the 6.0 kg block ($6.0 \times 6.0$), not the contact force.
perOption.C: Not obtained from a consistent force analysis.
perOption.D: Takes $54 - 6.0$, the net force on the whole system.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q6.issues: Stem says friction is 'between the blocks and the surface' but the diagram puts the 6.0 N on the 6.0 kg block only. Key 12 N requires all friction on the 6.0 kg block; if friction were shared by mass the answer would be 13.5 N (not an option).

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
At the top, tension and weight both point towards the centre: $T + mg = \frac{mv^2}{r}$.

$\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{0.10 \times 6.0^2}{0.50} = 7.2\ \mathrm{N}$, so $T = 7.2 - 0.98 = 6.2\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: This is just the weight $mg$.
perOption.B: Correct. $T = mv^2/r - mg$.
perOption.C: This is the required centripetal force, ignoring weight.
perOption.D: Adds weight ($T = mv^2/r + mg$), which applies at the bottom of the circle.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
O is equidistant ($r$) from all three planets. Split Z's mass into $M + M$: three equal masses $M$ at the vertices give zero net field at the centre by symmetry.

What remains is the field of the extra $M$ at Z: $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$ towards Z.

(Equivalently, the fields from X and Y, each $GM/r^2$ at $120^\circ$, sum to $GM/r^2$ pointing away from Z; Z gives $2GM/r^2$ towards Z.)

perOption.A: Masses are unequal, so the fields do not cancel.
perOption.B: The net field points towards the heavier planet Z, not X.
perOption.C: Correct. Net field $GM/r^2$ towards Z.
perOption.D: Treats the X and Y fields as $60^\circ$ apart (resultant $\sqrt{3}GM/r^2$); they are $120^\circ$ apart, giving $GM/r^2$.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q8.issues: Key gives D but derived answer is C. The fields from X and Y at the centroid are 120° apart, so their resultant is $GM/r^2$ (not $\sqrt{3}GM/r^2$); net field = $2GM/r^2 - GM/r^2 = GM/r^2$ towards Z. Key appears wrong.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Potential is a scalar, so contributions simply add: $\phi = -\frac{GM}{r} - \frac{GM}{r} - \frac{2GM}{r} = -\frac{4GM}{r}$.

Being a scalar, it has no direction.

perOption.A: Potentials are all negative and add; they cannot cancel.
perOption.B: Potential is a scalar with no direction, and the sum is not $-GM/r$.
perOption.C: Gravitational potential is negative and has no direction.
perOption.D: Correct. $-4GM/r$, scalar.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body:
$E = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$ with $\omega = 2\pi/T$.

Tripling $T$ makes $\omega^2$ one-ninth; doubling $x_0$ makes $x_0^2$ four times. New energy $= 18 \times \tfrac{4}{9} = 8\ \mathrm{mJ}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $18 \times 4/9$.
perOption.B: Uses $\omega$ not squared and amplitude not squared: $18 \times 2/3$.
perOption.C: Doubles the energy for doubled amplitude and ignores the period.
perOption.D: Squares the amplitude factor but ignores the period change.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
After W the light is plane-polarised with intensity $\tfrac{1}{2}I_0$.

Malus' law uses the angle between successive axes: W to X is $40^\circ-30^\circ=10^\circ$, X to Y is $60^\circ-40^\circ=20^\circ$.

$I = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0\cos^2 10^\circ\cos^2 20^\circ = 0.5(0.970)(0.883)I_0 \approx 0.43I_0$.

perOption.A: Does not follow from halving then applying $\cos^2$ to the angle between successive axes; typically from using the absolute axis angles.
perOption.B: Results from using a wrong angle between successive axes (e.g. measuring Y relative to W) instead of $10^\circ$ and $20^\circ$.
perOption.C: Correct. $0.5\cos^2 10^\circ\cos^2 20^\circ I_0 \approx 0.43I_0$.
perOption.D: Too large; overestimates transmission, e.g. by mishandling the initial factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ or the angles.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q11.issues: Diagram angles are not drawn to scale (drawn lines differ noticeably from the labelled 30°, 40°, 60°); solution uses the labels.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
$I \propto A^2$, so doubling the amplitude gives intensity $4I$ over area $S$, i.e. power $4IS$.

Focusing all this power onto $\tfrac{1}{3}S$ gives $I' = \dfrac{4IS}{S/3} = 12I$.

perOption.A: Takes $I \propto A$ (factor 2) and multiplies by 3.
perOption.B: Correct. $4 \times 3 = 12$.
perOption.C: Uses a factor of 9 for the area (squaring the area ratio) with factor 2 for amplitude.
perOption.D: Multiplies by 8 (cubing the amplitude ratio) and then by 3, or double counts the factor of 2.

perOption.A: Half the correct value, e.g. from using $2b$ or halving the angle.
perOption.B: Correct. $s = (\lambda/b)d$.
perOption.C: Divides the distance by the angle (and halves it) instead of multiplying.
perOption.D: Divides the distance by the angle, $d/\theta$, instead of multiplying.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
Mean KE $\tfrac{1}{2}m\langle c^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}kT$, so $c_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$.

Doubling $T$ multiplies $c_{rms}$ by $\sqrt{2}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $c_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$.
perOption.B: Assumes $c_{rms} \propto T$; it is the mean kinetic energy, not the speed, that doubles.
perOption.C: Assumes $c_{rms} \propto T^{3/2}$, which has no basis.
perOption.D: Assumes $c_{rms} \propto T^2$, inverting the square-root relationship.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
The containers are connected, so at equilibrium the gas has the same pressure $p$ in both.

From $pV = nRT$, $n = \dfrac{pV}{RT}$, so $n \propto \dfrac{V}{T}$.

$\dfrac{n_X}{n_Y} = \dfrac{2V/2T}{V/T} = 1.00$.

(The answer key gives A, 0.25; this does not follow from the ideal gas law with equal pressures.)

perOption.A: Key's answer, but $0.25$ would require $n \propto T/V$ inverted on both factors, e.g. $\dfrac{V/2T}{2V/T}$; it does not follow from $pV=nRT$ with equal pressure.
perOption.B: Correct. Equal pressure and equal $V/T$ give a ratio of 1.
perOption.C: Considers only the volume ratio and ignores the temperature difference.
perOption.D: Multiplies the volume and temperature ratios ($2\times2$) instead of dividing.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: Answer disagreement: key says A (0.25) but with equal pressure in the connected containers $n \propto V/T$ gives $n_X/n_Y = (2V/2T)/(V/T) = 1.00$ (B). Key appears to be wrong; please verify.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
Energy to warm ice to $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $0.100(2100)(10.0) = 2100\ \mathrm{J}$.

Energy released by water cooling to $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $0.150(4180)(20.0) = 12\,540\ \mathrm{J}$.

This is not enough to melt all the ice ($0.100\times334\,000 = 33\,400\ \mathrm{J}$), so the mixture ends at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Energy left for melting $= 10\,440\ \mathrm{J}$, melting $10\,440/334\,000 = 31.3\ \mathrm{g}$, so $100 - 31.3 = 68.7\ \mathrm{g}$ of ice remains.

perOption.A: 0 K is absolute zero, not the melting point; and 31.3 g is the mass melted, not remaining.
perOption.B: Correct mass but 0 K is absolute zero; the mixture is at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (273 K).
perOption.C: 31.3 g is the mass of ice that melts, not the mass remaining.

Peak power in $R$: $P_0 = \dfrac{V_0^2}{R} = \dfrac{12.0^2}{50} = 2.88\ \mathrm{W}$.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
The 2 μF capacitor on AB is directly across the battery; the 2 μF (AC) and 3 μF (CB) capacitors form a series branch also across 5.0 V.

The forces between the wires form a Newton's third law pair, so they are equal in magnitude whatever the two currents are.

280 days is two half-lives, so $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of the original nuclei decay.

Each decay loses only an alpha particle (mass ≈ 4 u); the 206 u daughter stays in the sample. For $N$ initial nuclei of mass 210 u, mass lost $= \tfrac{3}{4}N\times4\ \mathrm{u} = 3N\ \mathrm{u}$.

Beta particles penetrate a few millimetres of tissue and are moderately ionising, so they deliver their dose near the surface, ideal for skin cancers and surface tumours.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
Potential difference is work done per unit charge: $V = W/Q$.

Work has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$ and charge $Q = It$ has units $\mathrm{A\,s}$.

So $\mathrm{V} = \dfrac{\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{A\,s}} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,A^{-1}\,s^{-3}}$.

perOption.A: Dimensionally correct ($V = IR$) but the ohm is a derived unit, not a base unit.
perOption.B: Equivalent to the volt but contains the coulomb and ohm, which are derived units.
perOption.C: Correct. Expresses the volt entirely in kg, m, A and s.
perOption.D: Equivalent to the volt but the coulomb is a derived unit ($\mathrm{A\,s}$), not a base unit.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
Acceleration is the gradient of the $v$–$t$ graph. The gradient is zero at the peak and the trough of the curve.

At these points $|v|$ is a maximum, so the speed is greatest exactly when the acceleration is zero.

perOption.A: Velocity is also zero at $t = 0$ and $t = T$, where displacement is smallest, so the displacement is not greatest whenever $v = 0$.
perOption.B: Direction changes when the velocity is zero (graph crosses the time axis), not when the acceleration is zero.
perOption.C: Displacement increases whenever the velocity is positive, which includes times when the gradient (acceleration) is negative.
perOption.D: Correct. Zero gradient occurs at the maximum and minimum of $v$, where speed peaks.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
Descending with $a = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downward: $Mg - L = 2M$, so $L = M(g - 2) = 7.81M$.

Ascending with new mass $m$: $L - mg = 4m$, so $m = \dfrac{L}{g + 4} = \dfrac{7.81M}{13.81} = 0.566M$.

Mass removed $= M - 0.566M \approx 0.43M$.

perOption.A: Too small; does not correspond to a correct application of $F = ma$ in both cases.
perOption.B: Correct. $M - L/(g+4) = 0.43M$.
perOption.C: This is the remaining mass $0.57M$, not the mass removed.
perOption.D: Too large; would leave a mass of only $0.14M$, giving an upward acceleration far above $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Take moments about B: $F_A(5.0) = 880(4.2) + 200(2.5)$, so $F_A = 839\ \mathrm{N}$.

Vertical equilibrium: $F_B = 880 + 200 - 839 = 241\ \mathrm{N}$.

$F_A/F_B = 839/241 \approx 3.5$.

perOption.A: This is $F_B/F_A$, the inverse ratio.
perOption.B: This is $F_A$ divided by the total weight (1080 N), not by $F_B$.
perOption.C: Correct. $F_A = 839\ \mathrm{N}$, $F_B = 241\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.D: This is the total weight divided by $F_B$, not $F_A/F_B$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Extension under 15 N is $90 - 60 = 30\ \mathrm{mm}$, so $k = 15/30 = 0.50\ \mathrm{N\,mm^{-1}}$.

At the limit of proportionality, $F = kx = 0.50 \times 100 = 50\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Uses the stretched length 90 mm instead of the extension: $15 \times 100/90$.
perOption.B: Correct. $F = 0.50\ \mathrm{N\,mm^{-1}} \times 100\ \mathrm{mm}$.
perOption.C: Uses the total length at the limit (160 mm) instead of the extension of 100 mm.
perOption.D: Does not follow from $F = kx$ with the correct $k$ and extension.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
At equilibrium the spring tension equals $mg$ and the extension is $y - x$.

Elastic potential energy is the area under the force–extension graph: $E = \tfrac{1}{2}Fx = \tfrac{1}{2}mg(y - x)$.

perOption.A: Correct. Area of the triangle under the $F$–$x$ graph.
perOption.B: This is the gravitational potential energy lost by the mass; only half of it is stored in the spring.
perOption.C: Squaring the extension gives wrong units; the $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ form needs $k$, not $mg$.
perOption.D: Wrong units and omits the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
Heat from friction $= fs = 30 \times 3.0 = 90\ \mathrm{J}$.

Work done by the pull $= 80 \times 3.0 = 240\ \mathrm{J}$. Gain in GPE $= 40 \times 3.0\sin 30^\circ = 60\ \mathrm{J}$.

Gain in KE $= 240 - 90 - 60 = 90\ \mathrm{J}$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
All points on a rigid disc share the same angular velocity, so Y has the same period, $3.2\ \mathrm{s}$.

With $v = r\omega$ and Y at radius $r/2$, $v_Y = \tfrac{1}{2}(1.0) = 0.50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
For a circular orbit $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$: smaller $r$ gives larger $v$.

The period $T = 2\pi r/v \propto r^{3/2}$, so it decreases.

The total energy $-GMm/2r$ falls; KE rises while GPE falls by twice as much.

perOption.A: Correct. $v \propto r^{-1/2}$ and $T \propto r^{3/2}$.
perOption.B: Speed increases in a lower orbit, and the gravitational force $\propto 1/r^2$ increases.
perOption.C: KE increases and GPE decreases (becomes more negative) in a lower orbit.
perOption.D: Drag removes energy so total energy decreases, and the period decreases.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body:
At height $3R$ above the surface the distance from Earth's centre is $4R$.

Weight $\propto 1/r^2$: $W' = W/4^2 = W/16$.

Potential $\propto 1/r$: $\phi' = \phi/4$.

perOption.B: Potential uses $3R$ instead of $4R$ for the distance from the centre.
perOption.C: Weight is taken as $\propto 1/r$ instead of $1/r^2$.
perOption.D: Weight uses $1/r$ and potential uses $3R$ instead of $4R$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
At the same temperature the mean KE $\tfrac{1}{2}m\langle c^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}kT$ is the same for both gases.

So $v_{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$: $v_{Ne} = 1800/\sqrt{5} \approx 800\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

At constant volume $pV = \dfrac{m}{M}RT$ gives $m \propto p/T$.

Initial: 19 kg at $9.5p_0$, 280 K. Heating would raise the pressure above $10p_0$, so the valve opens and the final state is $10p_0$ at 300 K.

$m_f = 19 \times \dfrac{10}{9.5} \times \dfrac{280}{300} = 18.67\ \mathrm{kg}$, so $0.33\ \mathrm{kg}$ escapes.

$\cos\omega t = \tfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \omega t = \pi/3$, so $t = T/6 = 2.0/6 = 0.33\ \mathrm{s}$.

The bob starts slowly near the extreme, so it takes longer than half of the quarter-period.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:

$\cos^2\theta = 0.25 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = 0.5 \Rightarrow \theta = 60^\circ$.

Open at both ends: fundamental has $L = \lambda/2$, so $f = v/2L$.

Closed at one end: fundamental has $L = \lambda/4$, so $f' = v/4L = 0.5f$.

The two p.d.s always add to the e.m.f.: $v + V = E$, so the graph is a straight line of gradient $-1$.

At $R = r$: $V = v = 0.5E$. At $R = 3r$: $V = 0.75E$, $v = 0.25E$.

So the line runs from $(0.5E, 0.5E)$ to $(0.75E, 0.25E)$.
