jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
All the junctions on the central vertical wire are one node P. So the network is a block between X and P in series with a block between P and Y.

Between P and Y there are three resistors in parallel, or four if $S_3$ is closed: $R/3$ or $R/4$.

Between X and P the top resistor $R$ is always there. Closing $S_1$ adds a parallel path through the other resistors, which can only lower this block below $R$. With $S_1$ open the block is exactly $R$.

So the maximum is $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ all open: $R + R/3 = 4R/3$.

perOption.A: Every switch closed adds parallel paths: $0.6R + R/4 = 0.85R$.
perOption.B: Closing $S_1$ makes the X–P block $2R/3$, and closing $S_3$ makes the P–Y block $R/4$: $11R/12$ in total.
perOption.C: Closing $S_3$ puts a fourth resistor in parallel on the right, giving $R + R/4 = 5R/4 < 4R/3$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body:
The energy stored in the capacitor is $E = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$.

A constant fraction $k$ of this energy becomes gravitational potential energy: $mgh = k\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$.

So $h \propto V^2$, and a graph of $h$ against $V^2$ is a straight line through the origin.

perOption.A: Correct. $h = \dfrac{kC}{2mg}V^2$.
perOption.B: Would need the energy to be proportional to $V$, like charge $Q = CV$, not $\tfrac12 CV^2$.
perOption.C: $h \propto V^2$, so $h$ against $\sqrt{V}$ is a curve.
perOption.D: $h$ increases with $V$, so it cannot be proportional to $1/\sqrt{V}$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
The field and the wire are both horizontal, so the magnetic force is vertical (upwards here). The normal force halves, so the magnetic force equals half the weight.

$BIL\sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{1}{2}mg$

$B = \dfrac{0.5 \times 0.050 \times 9.81}{10 \times 0.20 \times \sin 60^\circ} = 0.14\ \mathrm{T}$

perOption.B: Uses $\cos 60^\circ$ instead of $\sin 60^\circ$.
perOption.C: Sets the magnetic force equal to the full weight $mg$ instead of $\tfrac12 mg$.
perOption.D: Uses the full weight and $\cos 60^\circ$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body:
Accelerating from rest: $eV = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $\dfrac{e}{m} = \dfrac{v^2}{2V}$.

Undeflected in crossed fields: $eE = Bev$, so $v = \dfrac{E}{B}$.

Substituting gives $\dfrac{e}{m} = \dfrac{E^2}{2VB^2}$.

perOption.A: Uses $v$ instead of $v^2$, i.e. forgets to square $E/B$.
perOption.B: Uses $v = B/E$, the inverted velocity-selector ratio.
perOption.C: Inverts the energy relation, giving $2Vv^2$ instead of $v^2/(2V)$.
perOption.D: Correct. $e/m = v^2/(2V)$ with $v = E/B$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body:
Each vertical arm of the U cuts field lines as the wire moves right, so each has an e.m.f. $Blv$ along it. The bottom section moves along its own length and has no e.m.f.

The two arms have equal length and the same velocity, so both e.m.f.s point the same way (from the bottom up to the top, or the reverse). Going from P down one arm and back up to Q, they cancel.

Equivalently, the flux through the U-shape does not change as it moves within a uniform field. The e.m.f. across PQ is zero at all times.

perOption.A: Shows a non-zero e.m.f. only while the wire accelerates. The e.m.f. in each arm depends on velocity, and the two arms cancel anyway.
perOption.B: Plots something like the acceleration of the wire. The arm e.m.f.s cancel whatever the motion.
perOption.C: Correct. The equal e.m.f.s in the two arms cancel between P and Q.
perOption.D: Follows the velocity of the wire ($Blv$ for one arm), ignoring the opposing equal e.m.f. in the other arm.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body:
A transformer works by mutual induction. The alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic flux in the iron core, and this flux links the secondary coil, inducing an e.m.f. there.

So the coils need magnetic interaction (no electrical connection), and the input must be a.c. so the flux keeps changing.

perOption.A: There is no electrical connection between the coils, and d.c. gives no changing flux.
perOption.B: Magnetic linkage is right, but steady d.c. gives constant flux and no induced e.m.f.
perOption.C: The coils are electrically insulated from each other. Energy passes by changing magnetic flux.
perOption.D: Correct. Changing flux from a.c. links the coils magnetically.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body:
The uncertainty principle links position and momentum in the same direction: $\Delta y\,\Delta p_y \gtrsim h$.

Narrowing the slit reduces $\Delta y$, so $\Delta p_y$ must increase. The electrons get a larger spread of vertical momenta, so the beam spreads out more vertically after the slit, as in single-slit diffraction.

perOption.A: Gets the trend backwards: a smaller $\Delta y$ means a larger $\Delta p_y$.
perOption.B: The slit limits the y-position, so it is $p_y$, not $p_x$, that becomes uncertain. Nothing makes the electrons accelerate.
perOption.C: Correct. Smaller $\Delta y$ gives larger $\Delta p_y$, so the beam spreads more.
perOption.D: The uncertainty principle applies to all particles, including electrons.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body:
The rings are an electron diffraction pattern. The carbon atoms act as a grating for the electrons' matter waves, which is evidence for wave behaviour of particles.

The de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$, so a lower $v$ gives a longer $\lambda$. A longer wavelength diffracts through larger angles, so the rings get larger in diameter.

perOption.A: The rings come from diffraction, not electrostatic repulsion, and their diameters increase.
perOption.B: The trend is right, but electrostatic repulsion cannot produce a ring pattern.
perOption.C: Right cause, but a lower $v$ gives a longer $\lambda$ and so wider rings.
perOption.D: Correct. Lower $v$ gives longer $\lambda = h/mv$, so larger diffraction angles.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body:
Subtracting the background of 300 per minute gives corrected counts of 744 (none), 738 (paper), 196 (aluminium) and about 1 (lead).

Paper makes no real difference, so there is no alpha. Thin aluminium removes most of the count and lead removes the rest, which is how beta behaves. With 1 mm of lead the count is just background, so there is no gamma.

So the source emits beta only.

perOption.A: Correct. Not stopped by paper, mostly stopped by thin aluminium, and nothing gets through lead.
perOption.B: Paper changes the count only from 1044 to 1038, which is within random fluctuation, so there is no alpha.
perOption.C: With lead the count is 301, just background. Any gamma would get through 1 mm of lead.
perOption.D: There is no evidence of alpha (paper has no effect) or gamma (lead count is background).

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body:
Each decayed Rb-87 nucleus becomes one Sr-87 nucleus. Per $1$ Rb nucleus now there are $0.062$ Sr nuclei, so originally there were $N_0 = 1.062$ Rb nuclei.

$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ gives $t = \dfrac{\ln(N_0/N)}{\lambda} = \dfrac{t_{1/2}\ln 1.062}{\ln 2}$

$t = \dfrac{4.88\times10^{10} \times 0.0602}{0.693} = 4.24\times10^{9}$ years

perOption.A: Treats decay as linear: $0.062 \times t_{1/2}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $N_0/N = 1.062$ gives $t = 4.24\times10^9$ years.
perOption.C: Takes $0.062$ as the fraction of the original Rb that has decayed, i.e. uses $N/N_0 = 0.938$.
perOption.D: Wrong by a factor of ten. It is larger than one half-life, which a 6% decay cannot be.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
$\tan\alpha$ is a pure number, so each term on the right-hand side must be dimensionless.

So $Q$ is unitless (degrees belong to $\alpha$, not to $\tan\alpha$).

$P/\sqrt{M}$ must be unitless, so $P$ has the units of $\sqrt{M}$: $\mathrm{kg^{1/2}}$.

perOption.A: $P$ must cancel $\mathrm{kg^{-1/2}}$, so it has $\mathrm{kg^{1/2}}$. And $Q$ adds to $\tan\alpha$, which is unitless.
perOption.B: $Q$ is right, but $P/\sqrt{M}$ would then have units $\mathrm{kg^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: $P$ is right, but $Q$ adds to $\tan\alpha$, a pure ratio with no degrees.
perOption.D: Correct. $P$ in $\mathrm{kg^{1/2}}$ and $Q$ unitless.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
At release $v = 0$, so there is no air resistance and $a = g$.

As speed increases, air resistance increases and the resultant force $mg - F_\text{drag}$ decreases, so $a$ decreases, steeply at first and then more gradually.

At terminal velocity the drag equals the weight, so $a \to 0$.

perOption.A: Acceleration must fall to zero at terminal velocity, not to a non-zero constant.
perOption.B: This is the shape of the velocity–time graph, not the acceleration.
perOption.C: Acceleration starts at $g$ (no drag at $v = 0$); it does not start from zero.
perOption.D: Correct. $a$ falls from $g$ towards zero as drag approaches the weight.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy before and after is the same. During contact, though, the spheres deform and some kinetic energy is temporarily stored as elastic potential energy. So the kinetic energy is not conserved throughout the collision, and B is the incorrect statement.

A is true: the total momentum is $2Mv - Mv = Mv \neq 0$, so the spheres can never both be at rest. C and D follow from Newton's third law: equal and opposite forces acting for the same time give equal and opposite impulses.

perOption.A: True statement. Total momentum $Mv \ne 0$ means both cannot be at rest at once.
perOption.B: Correct (it is the incorrect statement). KE dips during contact as it is stored as elastic PE.
perOption.C: True statement. Equal and opposite impulses give equal magnitudes of $\Delta p$.
perOption.D: True statement. This is Newton's third law.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Down the incline: $ma = mg\sin\theta - f$.

At $20^\circ$ the acceleration doubles:
$mg\sin20^\circ - f = 2(mg\sin15^\circ - f)$

$f = mg(2\sin15^\circ - \sin20^\circ) = 0.50 \times 9.81 \times (0.5176 - 0.3420) = 0.86\ \mathrm{N}$

perOption.A: Comes from an algebra error in setting up the simultaneous equations.
perOption.B: Uses $mg(\sin20^\circ - \sin15^\circ)$, the change in the gravity component, instead of solving the equations.
perOption.C: Correct. $f = mg(2\sin15^\circ - \sin20^\circ) = 0.86\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.D: This is the weight $mg$, not the friction.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Immediately after the cut the submerged volume has not changed, so the upthrust is unchanged. The weight has fallen by a quarter, so the resultant force is upwards.

The removed piece was the top-left part, so the centre of gravity of what remains moves to the right of the centre line. The upthrust still acts through the centre of the submerged volume, on the centre line. Weight acting down on the right with upthrust acting up on the left gives a clockwise moment.

perOption.A: Upthrust now exceeds the reduced weight, and the moment is clockwise, not anticlockwise.
perOption.B: Correct. Upthrust exceeds weight, and the CG is to the right of the line of the upthrust.
perOption.C: The direction of the moment is right, but upthrust (unchanged) now exceeds the reduced weight.
perOption.D: Upwards is right, but the CG moves right, which gives a clockwise moment.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
At constant velocity the resultant force is zero. Down the slope, the driving force $F$ and the weight component together balance the resistance:

$F + mg\sin6.0^\circ = 2000$

$mg\sin6.0^\circ = 1500 \times 9.81 \times 0.1045 \approx 1540\ \mathrm{N}$, so $F \approx 460\ \mathrm{N}$.

$P = Fv = 460 \times 30 \approx 14\ \mathrm{kW}$

perOption.A: Correct. $P = (2000 - mg\sin6^\circ) \times 30 \approx 14\ \mathrm{kW}$.
perOption.B: Ignores the weight component and uses $2000 \times 30$.
perOption.C: Adds the weight component as if the car were going uphill: $(2000 + 1540) \times 30$.
perOption.D: Comes from resolving the weight wrongly, e.g. using the full weight or the cosine component.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
Useful output power $= 0.25 \times 10 = 2.5\ \mathrm{W}$.

Work done lifting the load $= Fh = 20 \times 0.50 = 10\ \mathrm{J}$.

$t = \dfrac{10}{2.5} = 4.0\ \mathrm{s}$

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio, giving power over work instead of work over power.
perOption.B: Divides by the efficiency instead of multiplying, using $40\ \mathrm{W}$ of output.
perOption.C: Correct. $t = 10\ \mathrm{J} / 2.5\ \mathrm{W} = 4.0\ \mathrm{s}$.
perOption.D: Treats 20 N as a 20 kg mass and multiplies by $g$ again.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
At the top, both the tension and the weight point downwards, towards the centre. Together they provide the centripetal force:

$T + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $T = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} - mg$.

perOption.A: Sign reversed. This would give a negative tension for any real motion.
perOption.B: Leaves out the weight, which also acts towards the centre at the top.
perOption.C: Correct. $T + mg = mv^2/r$.
perOption.D: This is the tension at the bottom of the circle, where weight acts away from the centre.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Weight follows the inverse-square law with distance from the centre of the Earth.

At a height of $5R$ the distance from the centre is $R + 5R = 6R$.

$W' = W\left(\dfrac{R}{6R}\right)^2 = \dfrac{W}{36}$

perOption.A: Correct. Distance from the centre is $6R$, so $W/6^2$.
perOption.B: Uses the height $5R$ instead of the distance $6R$ from the centre.
perOption.C: Uses $1/r$ instead of $1/r^2$, and the height instead of the distance.
perOption.D: Orbiting objects feel apparent weightlessness, but the gravitational force on them is not zero.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body:
The loss of potential energy equals the work done by gravity: $E = mgx$, so $g = \dfrac{E}{mx}$.

The mass loses potential energy moving from P to Q, so gravity does positive work along PQ. The field therefore points from P to Q, to the right.

perOption.A: $E/x$ is the gravitational force, not the acceleration (force per unit mass).
perOption.B: $E/x$ is the force, and the direction is reversed: losing PE means the field points from P to Q.
perOption.C: Correct. $g = E/(mx)$, pointing from P to Q.
perOption.D: Magnitude is right, but losing PE from P to Q means the field points towards Q.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
The mean translational kinetic energy of one particle depends only on temperature: $\langle E_k \rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}kT$.

With $T = 27 + 273 = 300\ \mathrm{K}$: $\tfrac{3}{2}(1.38\times10^{-23})(300) = 6.2\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$.

The number of moles and the molar mass are not needed.

perOption.A: Uses $T = 27$ in °C instead of 300 K.
perOption.B: Correct. $\tfrac{3}{2}kT$ with $T = 300\ \mathrm{K}$.
perOption.C: A macroscopic energy far too large for a single atom; not the per-atom mean KE.
perOption.D: This is the total KE of all 2.0 mol, $\tfrac{3}{2}nRT \approx 7500\ \mathrm{J}$, not the KE of one atom.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
The flasks are connected, so the pressure is the same in both. From $pV = nRT$, $n = \dfrac{pV}{RT}$, so $n \propto \dfrac{V}{T}$.

$\dfrac{m_P}{m_Q} = \dfrac{n_P}{n_Q} = \dfrac{3V/200}{V/600} = 3 \times 3 = 9$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio (gives mass in Q over mass in P).
perOption.B: Treats amount as proportional to $T$ instead of $1/T$, partly cancelling the volume factor.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two factors (volume or temperature), not both.
perOption.D: Correct. Volume factor 3 times temperature factor 3.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
By the first law, $\Delta U = Q + W$. Internal energy can be raised by work done on the system (e.g. compressing a gas) with $Q = 0$.

So internal energy can increase without any heating.

perOption.A: During a phase change $U$ increases (potential energy rises) while temperature stays constant.
perOption.B: Correct. Work done on the system can increase $U$ with no heating.
perOption.C: Equal internal energy does not imply equal temperature; it depends on amount and type of substance.
perOption.D: $Q + W$ gives the change in internal energy, not the internal energy itself.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
Large amplitude means resonance: the bumps must drive the suspension at its natural frequency of $2.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

The car must cross 2 bumps per second, so $v = fd = 2.0 \times 5.0 = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Not a resonance speed; does not come from $v = fd$.
perOption.B: Computes $d/f$ instead of $fd$.
perOption.C: Uses one bump per second, ignoring the 2.0 Hz frequency.
perOption.D: Correct. $v = fd = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
A damping force opposes motion, slowing the oscillator, so the damped frequency is lower than the natural frequency. More damping lowers it further.

For a lightly-damped system the amplitude decays gradually but the period stays constant over time.

perOption.A: Correct. Greater damping slightly reduces the frequency.
perOption.B: Damping does increase the period, even if only slightly for light damping.
perOption.C: Energy is lost to damping, so the amplitude decreases over time.
perOption.D: The period is constant over time; only the amplitude decays.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: Option B is the common H2 approximation (light damping barely changes the period); the key's A relies on the strict result that damping lowers frequency. Defensible, but reviewers may want to note the subtlety.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
Reduced by 30% means the new intensity is $0.70I$. By Malus' law, $\cos^2\theta = 0.70$, so $\cos\theta = \pm0.837$ and $\theta = 33.2°$ (or $146.8°$, $213.2°$, $326.8°$).

Rotating by $180° + 33° = 213°$ gives the same result, since $\cos^2$ repeats every $180°$.

perOption.A: Correct. $\cos^2 213° = \cos^2 33° \approx 0.70$.
perOption.B: $\cos^2 226° = \cos^2 46° \approx 0.48$, a reduction of about 52%.
perOption.C: $\cos^2 237° \approx 0.30$: intensity reduced to 30%, not by 30%.
perOption.D: $\cos^2 253° \approx 0.09$, far too large a reduction.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
Intensity $\propto$ amplitude$^2$, so halving the intensity reduces the amplitude by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$: from 3 squares to about $3/\sqrt{2} \approx 2.1$ squares.

The frequency (pitch) is unchanged, so the period stays the same. Graph D shows amplitude about 2 squares with the same period.

perOption.A: Frequency doubled; changing intensity does not change frequency.
perOption.B: Amplitude unchanged and frequency increased.
perOption.C: Amplitude halved (1.5 squares), which would quarter the intensity.
perOption.D: Correct. Amplitude reduced by $\sqrt{2}$, same period.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body:
Rayleigh criterion: $\theta_{min} \approx \dfrac{\lambda}{b} = \dfrac{500\times10^{-9}}{25\times10^{-3}} = 2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

Separation on the object: $x = L\theta = 9.0 \times 2.0\times10^{-5} = 1.8\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.18\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Half the correct value, e.g. from using $2b$ or halving the angle.
perOption.B: Correct. $x = L\lambda/b = 0.18\ \mathrm{mm}$.
perOption.C: Not consistent with $\theta = \lambda/b$ and $L = 9.0\ \mathrm{m}$; a unit or substitution error.
perOption.D: Far too large; results from a unit conversion error.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Each charge gives the same field magnitude $E_0$ at the centre, pointing away from $+q$ and towards $-q$.

In C, the $+q$ (top-left) and $-q$ (bottom-right) on one diagonal both give fields towards bottom-right: $2E_0$. Likewise the other diagonal gives $2E_0$ towards top-right. These are perpendicular, so $E = 2\sqrt{2}E_0$.

D gives only $2E_0$; A and B give zero.

perOption.A: Four equal charges: fields from opposite corners cancel, giving zero.
perOption.B: Opposite corners carry like charges, so each diagonal cancels: zero.
perOption.C: Correct. Two perpendicular contributions of $2E_0$ give $2\sqrt{2}E_0$.
perOption.D: One diagonal (+q, +q) cancels; only the other gives $2E_0$.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body:
In time $t$ the protons in a length $vt$ of beam pass a point. If $N$ is the number per unit length, charge passing is $Nvte$.

So $I = \dfrac{Nvte}{t} = Nev$, giving $N = \dfrac{I}{ev}$.

perOption.A: $I/e$ is the number of protons passing per second, not per metre.
perOption.B: Correct. $I = Nev$.
perOption.C: Multiplies by $v$ instead of dividing; wrong units.
perOption.D: Omits the proton charge $e$; this is charge per unit length.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
When cold, the thermistor's resistance is high, so it takes the larger share of the 12 V. The heater must therefore be in parallel with the thermistor, i.e. the thermistor is in the arm connected to 0 V (B or D).

Current in the heater branch flows from the junction (higher potential) towards 0 V, so the diode must point towards the heater. Only D has the diode forward-biased.

perOption.A: Heater is across the fixed resistor, so it gets more voltage when hot, not cold; diode also reverse-biased.
perOption.B: Thermistor position is right, but the diode is reverse-biased so no current flows to the heater.
perOption.C: Diode is forward-biased, but the heater is across the fixed resistor, so it turns on when hot.
perOption.D: Correct. Heater across the thermistor with the diode forward-biased.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body:
Current: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t} = \dfrac{6.0}{120} = 0.050\ \mathrm{A}$.

P.d. across R: $V = \dfrac{W}{Q} = \dfrac{48}{6.0} = 8.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so the lost volts are $9.0 - 8.0 = 1.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

$r = \dfrac{1.0}{0.050} = 20\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Uses a wrong current (about 6 A), e.g. taking the charge as the current.
perOption.B: Uses $t = 2.0$ instead of 120 s, giving $I = 3.0\ \mathrm{A}$.
perOption.C: Correct. $r = 1.0\ \mathrm{V} / 0.050\ \mathrm{A}$.
perOption.D: This is the external resistance $R = 8.0/0.050$, not $r$.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: Stem says 'electromagnetic force' instead of 'electromotive force' (typo in the source).

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $Bqv = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r = \dfrac{mv}{Bq}$.

Period $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{Bq}$. The speed cancels: a faster particle moves on a proportionally larger circle.

perOption.A: $T \propto m$, so the period does depend on mass.
perOption.B: $T \propto 1/q$, so it depends on charge.
perOption.C: $T \propto 1/B$, so it depends on flux density.
perOption.D: Correct. $v$ cancels in $T = 2\pi m/(Bq)$.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body:
Vertical acceleration: $a = \dfrac{eE}{m} = \dfrac{(1.60\times10^{-19})(20000)}{9.11\times10^{-31}} = 3.51\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (towards the high-potential plate).

Starting with zero vertical velocity: $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(3.51\times10^{15})(4.0\times10^{-9})^2 = 0.0281\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Absurdly small; results from using the force $eE$ (or omitting the mass) rather than $a = eE/m$.
perOption.B: Also uses an incorrect acceleration, e.g. a force-based value, not $eE/m$.
perOption.C: Correct. $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(eE/m)t^2$.
perOption.D: Too large; mixes in the horizontal motion or omits the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ with a wrong acceleration.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body:
For a square wave, $I^2 = I_0^2$ at all times, so $I_{rms} = I_0$ and $P = I_0^2R$.

Doubling the peak current gives $P' = (2I_0)^2R = 4P$.

perOption.A: Ignores the change in current entirely.
perOption.B: Wrongly applies a $\sqrt{2}$ factor from sinusoidal a.c.
perOption.C: Assumes power is proportional to current, not current squared.
perOption.D: Correct. $P \propto I^2$.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$, so equal wavelengths require equal momentum $mv$.

The heaviest particle needs the smallest velocity: the helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons, about $4\,u$).

perOption.A: A proton (about $1\,u$) is lighter, so it needs a higher speed.
perOption.B: Correct. Largest mass, so smallest $v$ for the same momentum.
perOption.C: The electron is the lightest, so it needs the largest speed.
perOption.D: A neutron (about $1\,u$) is lighter than the helium nucleus.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body:
Each photon has momentum $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$. On normal reflection its momentum reverses, so the change is $\dfrac{2h}{\lambda}$.

With $n$ photons per second, the force is the rate of change of momentum: $F = \dfrac{2nh}{\lambda}$.

perOption.A: Uses $p = h\lambda$ and ignores the reversal of momentum.
perOption.B: Correct momentum per photon but treats the light as absorbed (no factor 2).
perOption.C: Factor 2 included but photon momentum wrongly taken as $h\lambda$.
perOption.D: Correct. Momentum change $2h/\lambda$ per photon, $n$ per second.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: A $\gamma$-photon carries momentum $h/\lambda$. The nucleus was at rest, so by conservation of momentum it must recoil in the opposite direction with equal momentum.

perOption.A: Stability depends on binding energy per nucleon, not total binding energy.
perOption.B: Such reactions can occur if enough kinetic energy is supplied to the reactants.
perOption.C: Correct. Momentum conservation requires the nucleus to recoil.
perOption.D: Radioactive decay is a nuclear process, unaffected by chemical reactions.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body:
Energy released = total binding energy of products − total binding energy of reactant.

$= 146(8.2) + 87(8.6) - 235(7.6) = 1197.2 + 748.2 - 1786.0 = 159.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

The free neutrons have zero binding energy.

perOption.A: Subtracts or adds per-nucleon values ($8.2 + 8.6 - 7.6 = 9.2$) instead of total binding energies.
perOption.B: Arithmetic or bookkeeping error in the total binding energies.
perOption.C: Mismatches nucleon numbers with binding energies per nucleon.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
$g = \dfrac{2h}{t^2}$, so $\dfrac{\Delta g}{g} = \dfrac{\Delta h}{h} + 2\dfrac{\Delta t}{t}$.

$\dfrac{\Delta t}{t} = \dfrac{0.0008}{0.4000} = 0.2\%$, so $2\% = \dfrac{\Delta h}{h} + 0.4\%$, giving $\dfrac{\Delta h}{h} = 1.6\%$.

perOption.B: Forgets the power of 2: $2\% - 0.2\%$.
perOption.C: Adds instead of subtracts, without the factor 2: $2\% + 0.2\%$.
perOption.D: Adds instead of subtracts: $2\% + 0.4\%$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
A football has a diameter of about $22\ \mathrm{cm}$, so $r \approx 0.11\ \mathrm{m}$.

$V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \approx \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(0.11)^3 \approx 6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$, which is of order $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$ (a few litres).

perOption.A: Too small: $10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3}$ is $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, the size of a sugar cube.
perOption.B: Correct. A football holds a few litres of air.
perOption.C: Too large: $0.1\ \mathrm{m^3}$ is 100 litres, about a large bin.
perOption.D: Far too large: $1000\ \mathrm{m^3}$ is the size of a building.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
The block is about to slip when the component of weight down the slope equals the maximum friction: $mg\sin\theta = \tfrac{1}{4}mg$.

So $\sin\theta = 0.25$ and $\theta = 14.5^\circ \approx 14^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct. $\sin\theta = 0.25$.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin\theta = 0.5$, i.e. friction equal to half the weight.
perOption.C: Uses $\cos\theta = 0.5$, mixing up the components.
perOption.D: Uses $\cos\theta = 0.25$, resolving the weight with cosine instead of sine.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Let the hexagon side be $a$. The 200 N force acts along BA, whose perpendicular distance from O is the height of an equilateral triangle, $\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a$.

$P$ acts perpendicular to OD at distance $a$. For no rotation: $P\,a = 200 \times \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a$, so $P = 173\ \mathrm{N} \approx 170\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Uses a moment arm of $a/2$ for the 200 N force.
perOption.B: Correct. $P = 200\cos30^\circ$.
perOption.C: Takes the moment arm as OB $= a$, ignoring that the force is not perpendicular to OB.
perOption.D: Divides instead of multiplies: $200/\cos30^\circ$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
On a smooth slope both masses have the same acceleration $g\sin30^\circ$ down the slope, so their relative acceleration is zero.

Their relative speed stays at $4.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and they start $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$ apart, so $t = 5.00/4.00 = 1.25\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Gives too early a time, as if A's deceleration were ignored while B accelerates (or the accelerations were not cancelled correctly).
perOption.B: Correct. Relative acceleration is zero.
perOption.C: Inconsistent with the uniform relative speed of 4.00 m/s over 5.00 m.
perOption.D: Too late; treats the masses as closing more slowly than their constant relative speed.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.issues: Stem says A and B are at 'the top and bottom' respectively, but the text and diagram place A at the bottom and B at the top.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
Each bead falls freely from rest, so it lands at $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$. For landing times $0, T, 2T, 3T, 4T$, the heights must be in the ratio $0 : 1 : 4 : 9 : 16$.

In D the beads are 0, 1, 4, 9 and 16 tick marks above the floor, so the sounds are equally spaced in time.

perOption.A: Gaps shrink going up (6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 ticks), so later sounds come closer together still.
perOption.B: Equal spacing means each bead lands sooner after the previous one, so intervals decrease.
perOption.C: Gaps grow linearly (1, 2, 3, ... ticks), but heights must grow as $n^2$, not as triangular numbers.
perOption.D: Correct. Heights are $1:4:9:16$, i.e. $h \propto t^2$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
Useful output power $= 0.40 \times 800 = 320\ \mathrm{W}$.

At constant velocity the driving force equals the resistive force: $F = P/v = 320/13 \approx 25\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Uses output power 320 W.
perOption.B: Uses the wasted power (480 W) instead of the useful power.
perOption.C: Uses the full input power of 800 W, ignoring efficiency.
perOption.D: Multiplies or divides incorrectly (not consistent with $P = Fv$).

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
Friction provides the centripetal force: $f = mr\omega^2$. Both objects share the same $\omega$, so Q at larger $r$ needs more friction.

The maximum friction $\mu mg$ is the same for both, so Q reaches it first and slides first.

perOption.A: Friction is $mr\omega^2$, which differs because the radii differ.
perOption.B: P is at the smaller radius, so it needs less friction, not more.
perOption.C: Both objects rotate with the turntable at the same angular velocity.
perOption.D: Correct. Q needs the larger centripetal force.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Vertically $T\cos\theta = mg$; horizontally $T\sin\theta = mr\omega^2$. Dividing gives $\tan\theta = r\omega^2/g$.

So $\omega^2 = g\tan\theta/r$ and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4\pi^2 r}{g\tan\theta}}$.

perOption.A: Ignores the angle, as if the centripetal force were equal to the weight.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin\theta$ instead of $\tan\theta$ when dividing the two force equations.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Places $r$ in the denominator; this does not even have units of time.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: Options in the image show garbled function names ('gsinsin θ', 'gtantan θ'); read as sin θ and tan θ.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body:
For a circular orbit $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, with $r$ measured from Earth's centre. P is at $r = 2R$ and Q at $r = 4R$.

$v_P/v_Q = \sqrt{4R/2R} = \sqrt{2}$, so $v_P = \sqrt{2}\,v$.

perOption.A: Uses $R$ and $3R$ (heights above the surface) and inverts the ratio.
perOption.B: Inverts the ratio: the closer satellite moves faster, not slower.
perOption.C: Correct. $r_P = 2R$, $r_Q = 4R$.
perOption.D: Uses heights $R$ and $3R$ instead of orbital radii $2R$ and $4R$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by both ratios ($0.012 \times 0.25$) instead of dividing by the radius ratio.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Divides by $r^2$ ratio and so treats potential like field strength ($0.012/0.0625$).
perOption.D: Inverts the mass ratio.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
For SHM $a = -\omega^2 x$, so $\omega^2$ is the magnitude of the gradient of the $a$–$x$ graph.

$\omega^2 = 0.30/6.0 = 0.050\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}$, so $\omega = \sqrt{0.050} = 0.22\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: This is $\omega^2$, not $\omega$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $\sqrt{6.0/0.30}$, inverting the gradient.
perOption.D: Uses $6.0/0.30$, inverting the gradient and not square-rooting.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.issues: Graph axis label shows 'a / cms2' (missing the minus sign in cm s^-2); does not affect the answer.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
P is at a crest at $t = 0$, so $y_P = A\cos\omega t$.

S is at equilibrium. For a wave moving right, S copies the point to its left, which is below it, so S is moving down: $y_S = -A\sin\omega t$.

S is $\tfrac{3}{4}\lambda$ to the right of P, so the phase difference is $\tfrac{3}{4}\times 2\pi = \tfrac{3}{2}\pi$.

perOption.A: The relation for S is right, but $\tfrac{3}{4}\lambda$ corresponds to a phase difference of $\tfrac{3}{2}\pi$, not $\tfrac{3}{4}\pi$.
perOption.B: P starts at a crest, so it follows $\cos$, not $\sin$; the phase difference is also wrong.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: S starts at equilibrium, so its motion is a sine, not $-\cos$; $\tfrac{1}{2}\pi$ is also wrong for a $\tfrac{3}{4}\lambda$ separation.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The ω symbol is missing from the image (stem reads 'angular frequency ... is .' and options read 'sin t', 'cos t'); the leftmost part of the wave curve and axis labels look partly garbled/cropped.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
By similar triangles the second area is $16/2.0 = 8$ times as far from the source.

$I \propto 1/r^2$ gives $I/64$. Since $I \propto A^2$, amplitude $\propto 1/r$, giving $A/8$.

perOption.A: Uses $I \propto 1/r$ and $A \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$.
perOption.B: Intensity is right, but amplitude falls as $1/r$ (to $A/8$), not to $A/4$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the area ratio (64) as the distance ratio, squaring twice.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
The pipe shown is closed at one end, so $L = \lambda/4$ and $f = v/4L$. We need $\tfrac{1}{2}f = v/8L$.

An open pipe of length $L'$ resonates at $nv/2L'$. With $L' = 4L$ the fundamental is $v/8L = \tfrac{1}{2}f$.

perOption.A: Open pipe of length $L$: fundamental $v/2L = 2f$, too high.
perOption.B: Open pipe of length $2L$: fundamental $v/4L = f$, not $\tfrac{1}{2}f$.
perOption.C: Correct. Fundamental $v/8L$.
perOption.D: Open pipe of length $6L$ resonates at $nv/12L$; $v/8L$ would need $n = 1.5$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
Grating spacing $d = 1/500\ \mathrm{mm} = 2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$. A complete spectrum of order $n$ needs the longest wavelength to appear: $n \times 600\ \mathrm{nm} < d$.

$d/\lambda = 2000/600 = 3.3$, so orders 1, 2, 3 are complete on each side: $2 \times 3 = 6$ spectra.

perOption.A: Counts orders on one side only.
perOption.B: Correct. Three complete orders each side.
perOption.C: Includes the central maximum, which the question excludes.
perOption.D: Uses 480 nm ($d/\lambda = 4.2$) so counts 4 orders each side, but order 4 is incomplete.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.issues: Question number '16' is cropped off the image.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
Initially both are at the same $p$ and $T$, so B holds $8n$; total $9n$.

Finally the pressures are equal: $n_A' = \dfrac{pV}{R(353)}$, $n_B' = \dfrac{8pV}{R(283)}$, so $n_A'/n_B' = 283/(8\times353) = 0.100$.

$n_A' = 9n \times \dfrac{0.100}{1.100} = 0.82n$, so $0.18n$ moves from A to B.

perOption.A: Correct. Moles transferred = $n - 0.82n$.
perOption.B: Uses Celsius temperatures or another inconsistent ratio.
perOption.C: This is the amount remaining in A, not the amount transferred.
perOption.D: Uses Celsius temperatures (ratio 10/80), which is invalid in $pV = nRT$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body:
For each power, energy supplied = latent heat absorbed + heat lost: $P_1 = m_1 L + h$ and $P_2 = m_2 L + h$.

Subtracting removes $h$: $L = \dfrac{P_1 - P_2}{m_1 - m_2}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The heat loss $h$ cancels.
perOption.B: Ignores the heat loss $h$ to the environment.
perOption.C: Averages two results that both include the heat loss, so $h$ is not removed.
perOption.D: Adding the equations doubles $h$ instead of cancelling it.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Potential at R: $V = 2 \times \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = 2 \times \dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(-30\times10^{-6})}{0.20} = -2.7\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{V}$.

Work done by an external agent $= qV = (-1.6\times10^{-19})(-2.7\times10^{6}) = +4.3\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$ (positive, since the electron is repelled by the negative charges).

perOption.A: Wrong sign and wrong power of ten.
perOption.B: This is the potential at R in volts, not the work done on the electron.
perOption.C: Potential with the sign reversed; still not multiplied by the electron charge.
perOption.D: Correct. $W = qV$ with both negative.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The μ symbol is garbled in the image (shows '⌈C' in the stem and '-30 C' in the diagram); μC is required for any option to match. Option A prints 10^13 (positive exponent), probably intended as 10^-13.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body:
Let the side be $a$. Moving the charge from X to Y brings it closer to Z ($a\sqrt{2} \to a$) and further from W ($a \to a\sqrt{2}$).

Field at Z (in units of $kQ/a^2$): before, $1$ from W plus $0.5$ along the diagonal from X gives $\approx 1.40$. After, $1$ from W and $1$ from Y at right angles gives $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$, a small increase.

perOption.A: Y is closer to Z than X was, so the potential at Z increases.
perOption.B: The charges move further apart, so the electric potential energy decreases.
perOption.C: The charges move further apart, so the repulsive force decreases.
perOption.D: Correct. $|E|$ rises from about $1.40$ to $1.41\,kQ/a^2$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
$V_s = 25 \times \dfrac{1600}{200} = 200\ \mathrm{V}$ r.m.s.

$I_s = 200/150 = 1.3\ \mathrm{A}$ r.m.s. Mean power $= V_{\mathrm{rms}} I_{\mathrm{rms}} = 200^2/150 \approx 270\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the turns ratio (step-down instead of step-up).
perOption.B: Ignores the transformer and uses the 25 V supply directly.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Doubles the power, using the peak value $V_0 I_0$ instead of the r.m.s. product.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body:
Charge delivered by a constant current: $Q = It = (2.5\times10^{-6})(200) = 5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}$.

Capacitance: $C = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{5.0\times10^{-4}}{5.0} = 1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{F} = 100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

perOption.A: Off by a factor of 2.5; dividing $200/5.0$ and ignoring the current value gives 40.
perOption.B: Correct. $C = It/V = 100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.
perOption.C: Wrong factor and wrong prefix (milli instead of micro).
perOption.D: Treats the current as $2.5\ \mathrm{mA}$ instead of $2.5\ \mu\mathrm{A}$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
In each box the three capacitors share the same two vertical wires, so they are in parallel: $3C$ per group.

The two groups are joined in series: $\dfrac{1}{C_T} = \dfrac{1}{3C}+\dfrac{1}{3C}$, so $C_T = \dfrac{3}{2}C$.

perOption.A: Treats all six capacitors as being in series.
perOption.B: Treats each group as series ($C/3$) and the two groups as parallel.
perOption.C: Correct. Two $3C$ parallel groups in series give $1.5C$.
perOption.D: Treats all six capacitors as being in parallel.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body:
Ions leave a velocity selector undeviated only if $v = E/B$, so P and Q have the same speed.

In the magnetic field $Bqv = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} \propto \dfrac{m}{q}$.

$r_Q = 3.7 \times \dfrac{1.5}{2} = 2.8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Uses $r \propto m/q^2$ or similar wrong combination, shrinking the radius too much.
perOption.B: Correct. $r \propto m/q$ at fixed $v$.
perOption.C: Inverts the ratio, using $q/m$ ($3.7\times 2/1.5$).
perOption.D: Multiplies by both factors ($3.7\times2\times1.5$) instead of taking $m/q$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body:
From the force: $BL = \dfrac{F}{I} = \dfrac{10\times10^{-3}}{5.0} = 2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{T\,m}$.

The wire moves in SHM, so its maximum speed is $v_0 = \omega x_0 = 2\pi(90)(1.8\times10^{-3}) = 1.02\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Maximum e.m.f.: $E = BLv_0 = (2.0\times10^{-3})(1.02) \approx 2.0\ \mathrm{mV}$.

perOption.A: Uses $v = f x_0$ (omits $2\pi$), giving $0.32\ \mathrm{mV}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $E_{max} = BL\omega x_0$.
perOption.C: Omits $2\pi$ and also slips a factor of 1000 in the units of force.
perOption.D: Takes the force as $10\ \mathrm{N}$ instead of $10\ \mathrm{mN}$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body:
For a rotating coil, $E = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, so the peak e.m.f. $E_0 = NBA\omega$ is proportional to the rotation frequency.

Doubling the frequency halves the period and doubles the peak to $2E_0$. Graph D shows twice as many cycles with twice the amplitude.

perOption.A: Doubles the amplitude but keeps the same period.
perOption.B: Halves the amplitude while doubling the frequency.
perOption.C: Doubles the frequency but keeps the same amplitude, forgetting $E_0 \propto \omega$.
perOption.D: Correct. Both peak e.m.f. and frequency double.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body:
The threshold frequency $f_0 = \Phi/h$ depends only on the work function of the metal, so it is unchanged.

At the same frequency, greater intensity means more photons per second arriving, so more electrons are emitted per second.

perOption.A: Threshold frequency is a property of the metal and does not change; also more photons means more electrons.
perOption.B: Threshold frequency is a property of the metal and does not depend on intensity.
perOption.C: Higher intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons are emitted.
perOption.D: Correct. Threshold unchanged; emission rate increases.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body:
Photon energies: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. Blue ($450\ \mathrm{nm}$): $E \approx 2.8\ \mathrm{eV}$. Red ($650\ \mathrm{nm}$): $E \approx 1.9\ \mathrm{eV}$.

Potassium ($2.3\ \mathrm{eV}$): only blue light releases electrons, so the leaf rises for blue only.

Aluminium ($4.3\ \mathrm{eV}$): neither photon has enough energy, so the leaf never rises.

perOption.A: Blue photons ($2.8\ \mathrm{eV}$) are below aluminium's $4.3\ \mathrm{eV}$, so no emission from aluminium.
perOption.B: Correct. Only blue light on potassium gives emission.
perOption.C: Reverses the wavelength–energy relation, thinking red photons are more energetic.
perOption.D: Reverses the wavelength–energy relation for potassium and wrongly allows emission from aluminium.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body:
The alpha particles and the gold nucleus are both positive, so the paths bend away from the nucleus.

The particle passing closer to the nucleus feels a stronger Coulomb repulsion and is deflected through a larger angle. In A the lower (closer) path is deflected more steeply than the upper path.

perOption.A: Correct. Both repelled; the closer particle is deflected more.
perOption.B: The upper particle is shown undeflected, but it would still feel some repulsion and bend slightly.
perOption.C: Both paths are deflected by the same angle despite different distances from the nucleus.
perOption.D: Shows the paths bending towards the nucleus, as if attracted.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body:
P starts at its maximum and falls to half that value at about $t = 3$ years, so $t_{1/2}(\mathrm{P}) \approx 3$ years.

After about 15 years almost all of P has decayed, so D1 simply decays exponentially. Its number halves every 15 years, e.g. from about $t = 20$ to $t = 35$ years and again to about $t = 50$ years.

perOption.A: 20 years is not the halving time of D1's tail; it is close to where D1 crosses D2.
perOption.B: Correct. P halves in about 3 years; D1's tail halves every 15 years.
perOption.C: 6 years is roughly two half-lives of P (quarter of the initial value).
perOption.D: 6 years for P reads the time to fall to a quarter, not a half.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
Energy has unit $\mathrm{J} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$ and $\omega$ has unit $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (radians are dimensionless).

$k = \dfrac{2E}{\omega^2}$ has unit $\dfrac{\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{s^{-2}}} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $k$ is the moment of inertia, unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.
perOption.B: This is the unit of momentum, not $E/\omega^2$.
perOption.C: This is the unit of force; it uses the wrong unit for energy.
perOption.D: Multiplies by $\omega^2$ instead of dividing.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
$\rho = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{4m}{\pi D^2 t}$, so $\dfrac{\Delta\rho}{\rho} = \dfrac{\Delta m}{m} + 2\dfrac{\Delta D}{D} + \dfrac{\Delta t}{t}$.

Contributions: $m$: $0.5/265.2 = 0.2\%$; $D$: $2\times0.1/10.3 = 1.9\%$; $t$: $0.02/1.36 = 1.5\%$. $D$ contributes the most.

perOption.A: Mass has the smallest fractional uncertainty (about $0.2\%$).
perOption.B: Correct. $2\Delta D/D \approx 1.9\%$ is the largest.
perOption.C: $\Delta t/t \approx 1.5\%$ is close but smaller than the doubled contribution from $D$.
perOption.D: Resistance is not used to calculate density, so it contributes nothing.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
Extensions are measured from the natural length: $x_1 = 5\ \mathrm{mm}$, $x_2 = 15\ \mathrm{mm}$.

$\Delta E = \tfrac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2) = \tfrac{1}{2}(380)(0.015^2 - 0.005^2) = 0.038\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\tfrac{1}{2}k(0.010)^2$, taking the 10 mm change as the extension.
perOption.B: Correct. $\tfrac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2)$.
perOption.C: Omits the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.
perOption.D: Uses lengths 50 and 60 mm instead of extensions from 45 mm, or a similar extension error.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: A couple consists of two equal, opposite, parallel forces with zero resultant. Its torque is $Fd$, where $d$ is the perpendicular separation of the forces, and this is the same about any point.

perOption.A: Zero resultant force does not rule out a resultant torque (e.g. a couple), and the body could also be moving at constant velocity.
perOption.B: Correct. The torque of a couple is $Fd$ about any point.
perOption.C: Concurrent lines of action give zero torque, but the forces must also sum to zero for equilibrium.
perOption.D: If the two forces act along the same line, there is no turning effect.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
The ball starts from rest and its velocity becomes increasingly positive as it falls, so downward is positive here.

Q is the maximum downward velocity just before the first impact. The maximum upward velocity is just after the bounce, at R (largest negative value).

So D is the incorrect statement. A, B and C are true: area under PQ is the fall distance, speed after each bounce is less than before (KE lost), and the gradient of every straight segment is $g$.

perOption.A: True: the area under PQ is the distance fallen from rest, i.e. the initial height.
perOption.B: True: the rebound speed at R is less than the impact speed at Q, so kinetic energy is lost.
perOption.C: True: between bounces only gravity acts, so the gradient is $g$.
perOption.D: Correct (this statement is false). Q is the maximum downward velocity; the maximum upward velocity is at R.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
Mass of air pushed down per second: $\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \rho A v = \rho\left(\dfrac{\pi D^2}{4}\right)v$.

Power = rate of KE given to the air: $P = \tfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{dm}{dt}v^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\dfrac{\pi D^2}{4}v^3 = \dfrac{1}{8}\pi\rho D^2 v^3$.

perOption.A: Correct. $P = \tfrac{1}{2}(\rho A v)v^2$ with $A = \pi D^2/4$.
perOption.B: Uses $A = \pi D^2$, treating the diameter as the radius.
perOption.C: Omits the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in kinetic energy, giving $Fv = \rho A v^3$.
perOption.D: Gives $\rho A v^2$, which is the force (rate of change of momentum), not power.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
Work done by a force is the area under its force–displacement graph.

Work done against air resistance, which becomes thermal energy, is the area under the $R$ line, i.e. Q. Area P (between F and R) is the net work, which becomes kinetic energy.

perOption.A: P is the area between F and R: the net work, equal to the gain in kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct. Area under R is the work done against air resistance.
perOption.C: P − Q has no physical meaning here.
perOption.D: P + Q is the total work done by F.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
Vertically from rest: $y = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, so $t \propto \sqrt{y}$. Falling $4y$ takes $2t$.

Horizontal velocity is constant, so $x = u t$ doubles to $2x$.

perOption.A: Ignores that a greater height means a longer time of flight.
perOption.B: Correct. $t \propto \sqrt{y}$ so $x$ doubles.
perOption.C: Assumes $x \propto y$.
perOption.D: Assumes $x \propto y^2$.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
By Newton's third law, the force on Y equals in magnitude the force on X.

Change in momentum of X: $\Delta p = 2.5(6.0 - 2.0) = 10\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

$F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{10}{0.020} = 500\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Gives the impulse ($10\ \mathrm{N\,s}$) instead of dividing by the contact time.
perOption.B: Uses only Y's speed $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$: $1.0\times4.0/0.020$.
perOption.C: Uses X's final momentum $2.5\times2.0 = 5\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ instead of its change in momentum.
perOption.D: Correct. $F = 10/0.020 = 500\ \mathrm{N}$.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body:
The body leaves the track in the upper half, so it must rise above the height of the centre: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 > mgr$, giving $v > \sqrt{2gr}$.

It must not complete the loop. At the top it needs $v_{top}^2 \ge gr$, so from energy $v^2 \ge gr + 4gr = 5gr$ to complete it. Hence $2gr < v^2 < 5gr$, and only $\sqrt{4gr}$ fits.

perOption.A: With $v = \sqrt{gr}$ it only rises to $r/2$ and slides back down without leaving the track.
perOption.B: With $v = \sqrt{2gr}$ it just reaches the height of the centre with zero speed and slides back.
perOption.C: Correct. $2gr < v^2 < 5gr$.
perOption.D: $v^2 = 6gr > 5gr$, so it completes the loop.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
For a circular orbit, $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = mr\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$, so $T^2 \propto r^3$.

New period $T' = T(0.25)^{3/2} = 0.125T$. In time $T$ the planet completes $T/T' = 8$ revolutions.

perOption.A: Gives the new period as a fraction of $T$ ($0.125$), not the number of revolutions.
perOption.B: Assumes $T \propto r$ and gives the period ratio.
perOption.C: Assumes $T \propto r$, giving 4 revolutions.
perOption.D: Correct. $T \propto r^{3/2}$, so 8 revolutions.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
For a circular orbit, $\frac{GMm}{r^2} = m\omega^2 r$, so $r^3 = \frac{GM}{\omega^2}$. The satellite mass $m$ cancels, so satellites of any mass can occupy a geostationary orbit.

The statement that all geostationary satellites must have the same mass is therefore false.

perOption.A: True: the orbit must be centred on Earth's centre and stay above one point, so it lies in the equatorial plane.
perOption.B: Correct. Mass cancels in $GMm/r^2 = m\omega^2 r$, so any mass can orbit there.
perOption.C: True: it must match Earth's rotation period of about 24 hours (strictly one sidereal day).
perOption.D: True: fixed $\omega$ fixes $r^3 = GM/\omega^2$, so there is only one radius.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
The body starts at $x = 0$ (equilibrium), where speed is maximum, so $E$ starts at its maximum. $E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \propto \cos^2\omega t$, which is never negative and has period $T/2$: $E$ is zero at each extreme of $x$ and maximum each time $x = 0$.

Graph D starts at a maximum, touches zero twice per oscillation, and stays non-negative.

perOption.A: KE cannot be negative, and this just copies the displacement graph.
perOption.B: KE cannot be negative; this is a cosine with the same period as $x$.
perOption.C: Starts at zero KE, but at $x = 0$ the body moves fastest so KE is maximum at $t = 0$.
perOption.D: Correct. KE $\propto \cos^2\omega t$: maximum at $x = 0$, zero at the extremes, twice the frequency.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
Each particle undergoes SHM, so its acceleration always points towards its equilibrium position. Acceleration opposes velocity when the particle is moving away from equilibrium.

From the diagram, A is at maximum displacement to the right (velocity zero) and C is at its equilibrium position (acceleration zero). For a wave moving right, a particle copies the motion of the particle to its left: B is displaced left and moving right (back towards equilibrium), while D is displaced right and still moving right, away from equilibrium. So at D the acceleration (to the left) is opposite to the velocity.

perOption.A: A is at maximum displacement, so its velocity is zero.
perOption.B: B is displaced to the left but moving right towards equilibrium, so acceleration and velocity are in the same direction.
perOption.C: C is at its equilibrium position, so its acceleration is zero.
perOption.D: Correct. D is displaced right and moving further right, so the restoring acceleration opposes its velocity.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.issues: Answer depends on reading small displacements from the diagram; derived D from pixel positions, which agrees with the key.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
The curved lines are crests; troughs lie midway between neighbouring crests. Complete destructive interference happens where a crest from one slit meets a trough from the other.

Point C lies on a crest from one slit, exactly halfway between two crests from the other slit, i.e. on a trough. The two waves cancel there.

perOption.A: A is at the edge of a slit in the barrier, not in the overlap region of the two diffracted waves.
perOption.B: B is where crests from both slits meet (on the central axis, zero path difference): constructive.
perOption.C: Correct. A crest from one slit meets a trough from the other.
perOption.D: D is in the middle of a diamond between crests of both waves, i.e. trough meets trough: constructive.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
Angular separation $\theta = \frac{1\times10^{11}}{6\times10^{16}} = 1.7\times10^{-6}$ rad. Just resolved, so $b = \frac{\lambda}{\theta} = \frac{6\times10^{-7}}{1.7\times10^{-6}} \approx 0.36\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0.4\ \mathrm{m}$.

For red light, $\theta_{min} = \frac{7\times10^{-7}}{0.36} = 1.9\times10^{-6}$ rad, which is larger than $1.7\times10^{-6}$ rad, so the red stars cannot be resolved. Statement C is incorrect.

perOption.A: True: $b = \lambda/\theta \approx 0.36\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.B: True: $\theta_{min} \approx \lambda/b$ depends on both.
perOption.C: Correct (incorrect statement). Longer wavelength gives a larger $\theta_{min}$, so stars at the same angular separation are not resolved.
perOption.D: True: $3\times10^{-6}$ rad exceeds $\theta_{min} = 1.7\times10^{-6}$ rad, so they are resolved.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
Kinetic theory assumes random motion, negligible molecular volume, and no intermolecular forces except during (instantaneous, elastic) collisions.

It does not assume equal speeds: molecules have a distribution of speeds, and only the mean kinetic energy is fixed by temperature.

perOption.A: Correct. Molecules have a range of speeds; equal speeds is not an assumption.
perOption.B: This is an assumption: molecular motion is random.
perOption.C: This is an assumption: molecular volume is negligible compared with the gas volume.
perOption.D: This is an assumption: no intermolecular forces except during collisions.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body:
Internal energy is a state function, so over a complete cycle $\Delta U = 0$.

The cycle is clockwise on the $p$–$V$ graph (expands at $3\times10^5$ Pa, compresses at $2\times10^5$ Pa), so the gas does net work equal to the enclosed area: $(1\times10^5)(2\times10^{-3}) = 200$ J. Work done on gas $W = -200$ J.

From $\Delta U = Q + W$: $0 = Q - 200$, so $Q = +200$ J absorbed.

perOption.A: Sign error: in a clockwise cycle the gas does net work, so work done on the gas is negative.
perOption.B: Correct. $\Delta U = 0$, $W_{on} = -200$ J, $Q = +200$ J.
perOption.C: Wrongly adds the given $\Delta U$ values; $U$ returns to its starting value over a full cycle.
perOption.D: Wrongly sums $-600 + 150$ as the net $\Delta U$; over a full cycle $\Delta U = 0$.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Potential is a scalar, and all charges are at distance $r$, so $V_X = \frac{(6Q - 2Q)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{Q}{\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$.

Work done by an external agent to bring $+2Q$ from infinity is $qV = \frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$. The field does the negative of this: $-\frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$.

perOption.A: Forgets to multiply by the test charge $2Q$ (uses $+Q$).
perOption.B: Correct. $W_{field} = -qV_X = -\frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$.
perOption.C: This is the work done by the external agent; the field does negative work.
perOption.D: Counts all eight charges as positive ($8Q$) or doubles the potential incorrectly.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body:
Alpha particle charge $= 2e = 3.2\times10^{-19}$ C; $r = 0.10\ \mathrm{pm} = 1.0\times10^{-13}$ m.

$F = \frac{Q_1Q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} = \frac{(9.0\times10^9)(1.4\times10^{-17})(3.2\times10^{-19})}{(1.0\times10^{-13})^2} \approx 4.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Prefix/power error (e.g. not squaring $r$ correctly).
perOption.B: Uses $r$ instead of $r^2$ in the denominator.
perOption.C: Correct. $F \approx 4.0$ N.
perOption.D: Doubles the force, e.g. using $4e$ for the alpha particle charge.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.issues: Distractors A, B, D do not obviously map to specific errors; per-option reasons are best guesses.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
Current flows radially from the rod to the case through the liquid. The path length (rod to case) is fixed, while the area the current passes through is proportional to the depth $x$.

From $R = \rho l/A$ with $A \propto x$, $R \propto 1/x$.

perOption.A: Treats the depth as both length and something squared; no such dependence.
perOption.B: Treats depth $x$ as the length of the conductor, but current flows across, not along, the depth.
perOption.C: Correct. Depth sets the cross-sectional area, so $R \propto 1/x$.
perOption.D: Treats $x$ as setting a circular cross-section ($A \propto x^2$), but only the height of the current path scales with $x$.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body:
With a single break in a series circuit, no current flows, so there is no p.d. across any intact lamp. The whole supply voltage appears across the break.

If the third lamp's filament were the only fault, the voltmeter across it would read the full mains voltage, not zero. So that fault cannot be the only one.

perOption.A: Possible: a break elsewhere means no current, so lamp 3 has zero p.d.
perOption.B: Correct. A broken third lamp would show the full supply voltage across it.
perOption.C: Possible: no supply means zero current and zero p.d. across lamp 3.
perOption.D: Possible: the break carries the supply voltage, leaving zero across lamp 3.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
With each capacitor $C$: P is three in parallel, $3C$. Q is three in series, $C/3$. R is $C$ in parallel with two in series ($C/2$), giving $1.5C$.

Increasing order: Q ($C/3$), R ($1.5C$), P ($3C$).

perOption.A: Reverses the order, treating parallel capacitors as combining like series resistors.
perOption.B: Correct. $C/3 < 1.5C < 3C$.
perOption.C: Ranks P lowest, applying the resistor rules to capacitors.
perOption.D: Places R lowest; R ($1.5C$) is larger than Q ($C/3$).

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body:
$B_X = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.0)}{2\pi(2.0)} = 3.0\times10^{-7}$ T, directed in the plane of the page (perpendicular to XP).

$B_Y = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(6.0)}{2\pi(3.0)} = 4.0\times10^{-7}$ T, directed perpendicular to the page.

The fields are perpendicular, so $B = \sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.0^2}\times10^{-7} = 5.0\times10^{-7}$ T.

perOption.A: Multiplies the two fields instead of adding them as vectors.
perOption.B: Correct. Perpendicular fields add as $\sqrt{B_X^2 + B_Y^2}$.
perOption.C: Uses wrong distances or an incorrect vector combination.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes directly, as if the fields were parallel.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.issues: Distractor C (6.3e-7) does not map to a clear single error; per-option reason is a best guess.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body:
The rotating disc cuts the magnet's field, inducing eddy currents in the aluminium. By Lenz's law, the eddy currents oppose the relative motion between disc and magnet.

The magnet therefore experiences a force dragging it along with the disc, so it rotates in the same direction as the disc.

perOption.A: Lenz's law opposes relative motion, so the magnet is dragged with the disc, not pushed the other way.
perOption.B: Correct. Eddy currents drag the magnet to reduce the relative motion.
perOption.C: Aluminium is non-magnetic, but induced eddy currents still produce a force.
perOption.D: The drag acts steadily in the direction of rotation; there is no restoring force to cause oscillation.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body:
Power input $P = (60.0)(120) = 7200$ W. Secondary r.m.s. voltage $= 4500/\sqrt{2} = 3182$ V, so cable current $I = 7200/3182 = 2.26$ A.

Power lost $= I^2R = (2.26)^2(40.0) = 205$ W, which is 2.8% of 7200 W. So $97.2\%$ reaches the consumers.

perOption.A: Larger loss than calculated, e.g. from a wrong current in the cable.
perOption.B: Correct. Using r.m.s. current $2.26$ A gives 2.8% loss.
perOption.C: Uses the peak voltage 4500 V as r.m.s., giving $I = 1.6$ A and a 1.4% loss.
perOption.D: Underestimates the loss, e.g. by using peak values inconsistently.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body:
Each photon has momentum $p = h/\lambda$ and energy $hc/\lambda$. For power $P$, photon rate is $P\lambda/(hc)$, so force $= \text{rate} \times h/\lambda = P/c$.

The force depends only on power, not wavelength. With equal power and equal spot area, the pressure is the same: $p$.

perOption.A: Correct. Force $= P/c$, independent of wavelength.
perOption.B: Considers only momentum per photon ($\propto 1/\lambda$) and ignores the larger photon rate for red light.
perOption.C: Inverts the momentum ratio and still ignores photon rate.
perOption.D: Squares the wavelength ratio with no physical basis.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body:
The electron is described by a wavefunction $\psi$, and $|\psi|^2$ gives the probability density of finding it at a point.

The 'electron cloud' represents this probability distribution: denser regions are where the electron is more likely to be found.

perOption.A: The electron is not confined to a fixed radius; there is a spread of positions.
perOption.B: The probability density is not uniform; it varies with position.
perOption.C: The electron has no definite path; that is the classical Bohr picture.
perOption.D: Correct. It shows where $|\psi|^2$ is large.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body:
Live wood activity per gram $= 120/10.0 = 12.0\ \mathrm{min^{-1}\,g^{-1}}$; relic $= 8.05\ \mathrm{min^{-1}\,g^{-1}}$.

$\lambda = \ln 2/5730\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$, and $t = \frac{1}{\lambda}\ln\frac{12.0}{8.05} = \frac{5730}{0.693}(0.399) \approx 3300$ years.

perOption.A: Subtracts 195 MeV instead of adding it: $(1786-195)/236 \approx 6.7$.
perOption.B: Subtracts 195 MeV instead of adding it: $(1786-195)/233 \approx 6.8$.
perOption.C: Divides by 236 (counting the neutrons) instead of 233: $1981/236 \approx 8.4$.
perOption.D: Compares 120 with 8.05 directly without scaling to per-gram activity.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.issues: Distractors A and C do not map to clear single errors; per-option reasons are best guesses.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body:
Energy released = (total BE of products) − (total BE of reactants). Free neutrons have zero binding energy.

$(143 + 90)X - 235(7.6) = 195$, so $233X = 1786 + 195 = 1981$ and $X = 8.5$ MeV.

perOption.A: Subtracts the 195 MeV instead of adding it.
perOption.B: Subtracts the 195 MeV and spreads over the wrong number of nucleons.
perOption.C: Divides by 236 (including the neutrons) instead of 233.
perOption.D: Correct. $X = 1981/233 \approx 8.5$ MeV.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
A systematic error shifts all readings by the same amount, so the peak of the distribution is offset from $x_0$. A small random error means the readings are tightly clustered, giving a narrow peak.

Graph B shows a narrow peak displaced from $x_0$.

perOption.A: Narrow peak centred on $x_0$: small random error and no systematic error.
perOption.B: Correct. Narrow (small random error) and offset from $x_0$ (large systematic error).
perOption.C: Wide peak centred on $x_0$: large random error, no systematic error.
perOption.D: Wide and offset: large random error as well as systematic error.
